speakeroldname: Hon. Roy MacLaren (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
speechtext: that Bill C-8, an Act respecting the imposition of anti-dumping and countervailing duties, to amend the Currency and Exchange Act, the Customs Tariff and the Export and Import Permits Act and to repeal the Anti-dumping Act, as reported (with amendments) from the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, be concurred in.
Motion agreed to.
that the Bill be read the third time and do pass.

Mr. Speaker, by and large, this Bill follows the recommendations contained in the report of the Subcommittee of the Finance Committee on special import measures. Therefore, we are very much in favour of the Bill. In particular, the Bill proposes that the anti-dumping and countervailing duties legislation should place specific time limits on various stages of the investigation of dumping and subsidization, as well as the conduct of injury inquiries. To complete cases more rapidly, the Department of National Revenue's investigation of dumping and subsidization, and the Tribunal's inquiry into injury, should coincide to a greater extent than they do at present. Basically, those recommendations have been followed in Clauses 31, 32, 38, 41 and 43.
In the past when complaints have been laid it has been possible to use the favourite lawyer's trick when defending a matter-that is, to delay, delay and delay. As a consequence, the injury carries on. Even if a finding has been made that there has been dumping or undue subsidization, the damage has already been done and in many cases the Canadian industry will have gone under or will have been severely damaged to the point where even an order by the Tribunal would do nothing except tell that industry: "It is too bad that you are good Canadians and that you waited for this legislation to assist you, but now you are dead and we will send you roses; or we will send you the investigators from the Department of National Revenue, or the bankruptcy group from Consumer and Corporate Affairs to find out why you went under". Therefore, we welcome the proposal to move ahead and complete more rapidly the investigations and hearings of the Tribunal.
The second proposal which was made by the subcommittee reads as follows:
The new anti-dumping and countervailing duties legislation should permit the suspension of investigations if price undertakings have been accepted by National Revenue from exporters who are dumping, or price or quantitative undertakings from exporters and their governments in the case of subsidized exports to Canada.
That matter has been dealt with in Clauses 49 to 54 of the Bill.
Currency and Exchange Act
The third proposal which the subcommittee made was that the new countervailing duty procedure should generally parallel anti-dumping procedures. That raises two matters. First, there is an order on dumping which imposes a duty or charge that is an anti-dumping levy. Often the problem is not the dumping of goods but situations in which countries have subsidized their internal producers to the extent that the goods are for sale in their own country at an exceptionally low price. When those goods are shipped to Canada, those countries can properly say that they are not dumping the goods. For example, Italy can say that their tomatoes are for sale in Italy at the same price as they are offering them for sale in Canada. We could ask why canned tomatoes are so cheap in Italy. The answer is that they subsidize their farmers to grow tomatoes. In effect, the canned tomatoes are cheap because Italy also subsidizes their steel can makers. Therefore, the result is that tomatoes are a product which is exceptionally low-priced. If it is low-priced to Italians, then why can they not sell it at the same low price to Canadians? The answer is that Canadian farmers and can companies will be put out of business. Why is Italy able to do it? Not because their price of production is any lower-indeed, it is probably higher-but because the agriculture and steel industries are subsidized to such an extent that the products in those industries are coming into Canada at an unfair price marking. If we were to allow that to continue, we would seriously damage our farmers and our steel industry.
There is a problem in the country today with respect to wine. As many of us are aware from reading articles, some members of the European Common Market-the countries of Germany, France, Italy and Portugal-have been producing excellent crops of grapes over the last few years. The consequence is that they are virtually floating in a sea of wine. To a large extent this is because agriculture in Europe has been excessively subsidized by rebates on land taxation, subsidies of one form or another in terms of interest on loans to farm groups, acreage subsidies and the like. The effect is that subsidized agriculture ends up with enormous production. If producers have a good year on top of that, they wind up with enormous production.
Without some kind of protection, the Canadian wine industry would be wiped out. We could place certain tariffs on wine, but if we are prepared to sell it for virtually nothing, then it is a tariff on nothing. If fixed prices are placed on wine as is the case in Ontario, which indicates that foreign wine cannot be sold for less than domestic wine, then the pressure is still on and it makes it impossible for our own producers to produce. This legislation is exceptionally important as it gives another layer of protection and makes it possible for Canadian industry to be protected, not against ordinary and proper foreign trade-because I think we must recognize that we are a trading nation-but against subsidized imports and situations in which producers in other countries decide that our market is a place for their surplus.
The next proposal recommended that the anti-dumping legislation provide authority for the establishment in excep-

June 26, 1984
Currency and Exchange Act
tional circumstances of a basic price system. That is, I suppose, the philosophy of the legislation. When someone is bringing something to our country, the product which comes in must have a price structure which indicates that it could in fact be produced for the price at which it is offered. A constituent of mine informed me of a case recently which involved paint brushes in China. The brushes are made of hog bristles. They are good brushes. The fact is that the Chinese were selling paint brushes in our market at about half the price at which they would sell the hog bristles themselves. This is a case in which there is no basic price at all because there is no way of finding out what the market for paint brushes is in China. China does not have the same kind of society as Canada. They do not have hardware stores and the same merchandising system. The brushes were essentially made for one purpose: they were made for export. Hog bristles are also available for export. However, the brushes were coming into the country at significantly less cost than the brushes could have conceivably been made for if the hog bristles were worth what the Chinese were prepared to sell those bristles for.
Obviously, we must reach a fair price. This legislation will enable the establishment of a basic price. If we took the hog bristle price and the price at which China is prepared to sell those bristles and we added the price of putting a brush together, it would end up as a fair price. After all, China determines the price of the ingredient-the bristles. Why should that not be the basic cost of producing the brush? It is not a question of inquiring whether in fact it is a subsidy, because in a country where there is no market system it is difficult to determine whether it is a subsidy. There may be in fact no subsidy paid. It may be just the way the marketing system of that country values its product. On that basis, it becomes difficult to determine whether it is a subsidized import or whether it is dumped. What one has to do is to determine what is a basic fair value and charge duty accordingly or put on a countervailing duty or something of that nature, and this legislation provides for that.
With respect to the proposals, proposal No. 5 was the criterion for finding injury: the new definition of regional industry contained in international agreements or anti-dumping duties and on subsidies and countervailing duties should be taken into account by the Tribunal. That is dealt with in Clause 42(3) of the Bill. The recommendation was that the injury criteria specified in the GATT anti-dumping code be adopted into Canadian legislation as a reference for injury inquiries, and that the definition of "regional industry" contained in the GATT anti-dumping code should be taken into account by the Tribunal.
We live, Sir, as you know, in a very large country where we have five, six, and perhaps even more separate regions. The importation of an article at a very low price into one region of our country can hurt manufacturers in another region of our country where that importation is not taking place. Therefore, dumping or subsidization has to be looked at not only on the basis of the whole country, but on the basis of the regions of
the country. We are pleased that that particular provision is in the statutes.
Proposal No. 6 of the committee was that the existing Canadian legislation permitting imposition of import quotas based on injury findings by the Textile and Clothing Board or the Tribunal should be maintained. However, there should be provision to place the products on the import control list for monitoring purposes based upon the recommendation of the Tribunal and the Textile and Clothing Board. This whole question of imports and monitoring imports is dealt with in Clause 106 of the Bill and further dealt with on a three-year review period provided in Clause 104 of the Bill.
The next proposal was that Section 8 of the Customs Tariff should be amended to permit surtaxes to stay in effect for more than 180 days without parliamentary approval in the case where the Tribunal, or where appropriate, the Textile and Clothing Board, finds on a reference by the Government serious injury or threat of serious injury to Canadian producers. Clause 103 of the Bill provides for that but also provides that the review would have to be every three years instead of being an annual review. Therefore, there is provision in Clause 103 to make sure that the surtaxes can in fact stay in effect longer than the 180 days which was the case in the past.
Proposal No. 8 with respect to the legislation is that the legislative authority for applying surtaxes should also permit the application of surtaxes after certain quantities of the product have been imported. Again, if there is a quantitative import allowed, Clause 103 of the Bill provides that a three-year review should be held on those quantitative limitations. Proposal No. 8 of the committee was that the legislation should provide for specific authority for Canada to take safeguard measures for balance of payment purposes. Obviously, we live in a trading world but occasionally we can have, and have had in the past, balance of payment problems. We do not seem to have those right now, although I may point out to you, Sir, that in the first three months of this year we suffered a balance of payment deficiency. We have been very fortunate in our foreign trade to have a surplus of trade, and that has more than overcome our ordinary deficiency in terms of the tourist industry and our deficiency in terms of payments of interest and dividends to foreigners. However, we can, and have had in the past, serious problems with respect to balance of payments. Section 102 of the statute provides that we can interfere to safeguard our balance of payment problem.
Proposal No. 10 is that the Government should have the power to suspend or withdraw rights or privileges granted by Canada to other countries and to impose surtaxes, quotas or a combination thereof, or to impose countervailing duties, and in cases where it is deemed to be appropriate to respond to actions by foreign governments which either affect Canadian trade, goods and services or impair Canada's rights under trade agreements. That again is part of the provisions in Section 102.
There were some additional recommendations. First, that the Tariff Board should be empowered to undertake a review of decisions made by the anti-dumping tribunal when so

June 26, 1984

requested by consumer advocates and when, in the opinion of the board, it is in the national interest to do so. This was not completely done in the Bill, but Clause 45 of the Bill will permit interested parties such as consumers to make representations to the Anti-dumping Tribunal. Perhaps that ought to happen more often. But, of course, we are all consumers and it is difficult to get people interested in making representations to tribunals when the cost of going to a tribunal gets to be rather horrific in terms of legal fees and disbursements.
The subcommittee recommended further that there was a unique problem with respect to capital goods, and that problem continues. Clauses 89 to 95 of the Bill, to some extent, with regulations, perhaps help here. However, we may be building, for example, a transit system and another country may come in and make a bid on that transit system which is a one-of-kind item. In one-of-a-kind items it is very difficult to say whether an item is being subsidized or whether it is being dumped because, after all, if it is one-of-a-kind, how can you say it is being dumped in your country? So we always have a problem with capital goods because there is no specific market for a particular exclusive and unique type of machinery or equipement. It is on the basis that there must be some study made of it. We are not entirely happy with the way it is handled, but we will see how it goes. It may be impossible, really, to legislate here without interfering with the over-all requirement that we as trading nations should have our regulations for imports generally available to people to see and read and understand. We cannot have a situation where the Government is asked by some people to stop a foreign importer at the border because some Canadian all of a sudden objects that some foreign importer or manufacturer is bringing in goods cheaper than the Canadian thinks they can be produced. Indeed, world trade would cease to exist if the Government used that type of regulatory procedure, particularly when there is really no market for a product. It is exceptionally difficult on a capital goods matter to protect yourself. These clauses do something but we are not at all convinced that that is going to solve the problem, but again the problem probably defies a solution.
The subcommittee further recommended that the role of current import agencies be examined in relation to one another. That was not dealt with, but there are businesses in this country whose sole purpose is to buy foreign products, bring them into Canada and distribute them. They should be examined as to how they are working. We have not done it in this Bill and perhaps it should be done at some future time. The committee should continue to monitor the question of import regulation and control because after all, Sir, the question of goods coming into this country and their effect on jobs is pretty important to us. Therefore, the role that import agencies play in this country's trade patterns is important and has to be looked at continually.
There is provision concerning public disclosure in Clauses 78, 79, 82 and 88. The committee suggested that the legislation should outline a greater disclosure of information collect-
Currency and Exchange Act
ed by Revenue Canada during an investigation and the reasons underlying a decision. That is important. Importers are entitled to have the reasons why a countervailing duty is imposed, why the countervailing duty is 29.5 per cent or, in the case of the paint brushes I mentioned, in excess of 500 per cent. The committee also suggested that all confidential information be accompanied by a non-confidential summary. In other words, if there are matters brought to the Tribunal that are confidential, then surely they can be summarized in a non-confidential manner. It is not necessary to give away a company's trade secrets, but there is no reason why they could not be summarized in a non-confidential manner. The committee recommended that the Government be given the right to disregard any confidential information not accompanied by a non-confidential summary. Perhaps that is the way it should be. Then the committee recommended that the Government review all information claimed to be confidential in order to verify that fact. If it does not appear to be of a type that must be confidential, steps should be taken to convince the company to reclassify the information as non-confidential.
One of the greatest ways to avoid telling anyone anything, and we see it here in this House time and time again, is to say that the information is somehow confidential. Well, often what is confidential is just prejudicial. It is information that may cause the Government a great deal of distress, but it is not confidential. The recommendation is that it be handled in that fashion.
On balance, this is a worth-while Bill. I guess it goes against the grain of free trade, but I suppose in looking at legislation of this nature, we have to understand that while free trade is important, it also has to be fair trade. Too often we have been like boy scouts. We have said, "My goodness, we belong to GATT, we are free traders and therefore we will not step in when people take unfair action against us". Well, we have to realize that other countries subsidize their exports. We have to realize that other countries are prepared to use taxpayers' money to subsidize interest rates in order to finance capital goods. Some countries as a matter of national policy will encourage their steel industry to the extent where the importing country, such as the United States, is faced with a tremendous amount of steel imports and they are now looking at ways to reduce those imports. That is going to affect us. We should not be affected; we have been fair traders with the U.S. on steel. But when countries like Korea and East Germany dump steel in the United States at prices far below any realistic cost of production, then it becomes a question of unfair trade. When there is unfair trade, then we must be capable of protecting ourselves.
This Bill goes a long way toward making sure that trade remains free. At the same time that it makes sure that those engaged in unfair trading are stopped quickly. There will be a quick investigation, a quick order and a countervailing duty which redresses the balance. I commend the Bill to the House. I think it is important that it be passed, and it is essential that the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs continues to monitor the question of trading practices.

June 26, 1984
Currency and Exchange Act
It is a fast moving world out there. People are not afraid to take advantage of our relatively low tariffs and our open market. Canada is one of the few countries where it is not difficult to distribute goods. If you sold to Sears, Canadian Tire and Hudson's Bay, you have sold half the market or maybe even 80 per cent of the market in some goods. So you really do not have to hire a distributor who goes door-to-door across the country; it is much easier to merchandise products in this country. So when we allow importers that ease of access to our marketplace we must insist that they trade fairly. But we should have the same ease of access to the Japanese market as they have to our market. If we had that ease of access to the markets of Japan we would not have to impose the quota system which we have on Japanese automobiles because we too could sell our automobiles in their market. We could do as well in their market as they can do in ours. However, the ease with which they can get into our market is entirely different from the way we can get into theirs. I commend the Bill to the House on the understanding that the Bill and the trade activities be monitored over the years to come.

Mr. Speaker, some of what I will say today may appear to be a repetition of some of the remarks just made by the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I believe that they are worthy of further emphasis. I am not being critical, but I would like to draw some matters directly to the attention of the Minister who moved this Bill. I hope that it is possible for him to return because there are some serious problems in Canadian trade. There are some inequities which I think must be addressed by the Government. It is too late to address them through this or the preceding Bill, but I do think they deserve consideration.
Unfortunately, the negotiations which Canada has conducted on an international basis, and by which it has become a member of GATT, have not been conducted in a fashion which protects Canada against some of the unfair trade practices to which we are subject. As a result, goods are arriving on the Canadian market at prices which bear no relationship to our cost of production or to the cost of production in the export country. We have been weak. We have not protected ourselves as other nations have, either by artificial trade barriers or by agreement with our international partners in trade.
The steel situation is a prime example of what has happened to us. We have not protected ourselves in any way against being excluded from a market by virtue of the dumping of others. Yet that is exactly what we are experiencing with the United States today as it has decreed that there is injury when steel arrives in the United States from other countries at depressed prices. Although Canada has been able to prove that our prices are competitive, but not cutthroat, in respect of the steel market in the United States, we are excluded from exporting steel to the United States.
This could not be addressed in the discussions on the preceding Bill nor on this one. We must address this at the international trade level in a very serious fashion. Apparently
we have come up with a negotiated trade deal in GATT which only allows the total exclusion of the product concerned, whether from our market, the American market or others. Therefore, the innocent are classed with the guilty and punished in exactly the same fashion. We need further negotiations and further improvements in our international trade negotiations.
The former speaker mentioned wine. I think we can extend that to fruit juices and fruit juice concentrates such as from apples and grapes. The source from which they come and the terms and conditions under which they arrive here must be given serious consideration. The European Economic Community has subsidized the export of virtually all of its agricultural products. Canada has been a market for one or another of them at various times in virtually every year. Irish beef has been arriving in the Canadian market. European wines are presently arriving and will continue to arrive at prices which are more than competitive with the price of a comparable sized bottle of coke bought at the wholesale price. It does not make much sense that a bottle of wine can arrive in Canada at a price competitive with a bottle of coke produced in Canada because it involves a much more expensive process. That is implicit in the decision-making process which will decree that there is in fact injury to our Canadian market and dumping from foreign sources. We must address these problems.
I am not satisfied that by virtue of earlier negotiations this Bill does address that problem. There are literally billions of bottles of wine in excess of the European capability to consume which will have to be marketed somewhere in the world. Some of that wine is presently arriving in Canada at prices which bear no relationship to cost. However, because of the mechanism of indirect subsidy which was described in part by the previous speaker, we have not been able to establish a legal framework within which we can say that that wine is in fact being dumped in Canada. That is because the subsidy does not go directly to the farmer or the winery. It goes directly to the selling agency, whether that be a private broker or a private exporter. He is the one who receives the subsidy, and it is reflected in the price paid to the farmer for his goods or to the winery for its product.
This will just not work in the world of trade. Our wine industry would be a healthy one if given proper access to the Canadian market. It is small but it deserves consideration and reasonable protection, either by virtue of anti-dumping legislation or by renegotiation of the terms and conditions which apply to it. Either course may solve the problem. However, I do not believe we can solve it with this Bill, because I think it contravenes our agreement with GATT. It is merely a mechanism which was not defined in GATT. Therefore, it is not acceptable for us to accuse them of dumping. We must address these questions properly.
It is rather unique that the Member for Mississauga South would have so much to say in common with what I want to say. The Hon. Member mentioned brushes and hog bristles. He was talking about the largest single brush manufacturer in the British Commonwealth. That manufacturer is located in
June 26, 1984

the City of Saint John and has been subject to very unique pressures of pricing by foreign suppliers over the years. Its very existence has been threatened. This needs to be addressed. Such manufacturing does not exist in Toronto and therefore may not be addressed as it deserves.
I will also bring to your attention two tea packaging companies located in the City of Saint John. The consequence of inadequate protection for that industry may mean that it will fold up completely. It presently employs approximately 500 people in the reception of the raw product at the Port of Saint John and in its processing, packaging and sales operations. Every one of these jobs in the City of Saint John and the nearby town of Sussex is presently in jeopardy because the two companies find that they are exporting some of their product to the United States with a duty applied against exports to the United States. On the other hand, they are competing in the market in Canada on a duty-free basis with products from the United States packaged the same way. This spells the demise of these industries. This is one of the items which I would particularly like to draw to the attention of the Minister who has moved this Bill. It is imperative that he study it. The industry has made representations to the Government of Canada stating that in a few months it must make a decision whether to go out of business completely or to move the plant to the United States where it will have free access to both markets. The members of the industry say that they cannot exist in Canada when they are subject to duty on their exports to the United States but in competition with the same source of supply in Canada duty free. Free trade is a great thing, but I repeat the phrase of the Hon. Member for Mississauga South that fair trade is what Canada must accomplish in its negotiations and through its legislation. Nothing less can be acceptable.
I have yet to hear to what degree we will be able to apply this Act in its literal intention without being subject to penalty by our GATT trading partners. Is this Bill designed to be used in that fashion and does it set up any of the artificial trade barriers which have prohibited us from selling our wares abroad? For instance, it is impossible to get an agricultural product into the European market today unless it is something that they do not produce. Nothing that they produce can be imported except by special permit. However, Canada is open to virtually free trade on exports arriving from Europe in the same field. For example, recently I saw in the storage space of the Parliamentary Restaurant, a five-gallon can of fruit salad. There was a time when Canada would have made that fruit salad primarily from Canadian products. However, that product arrived in Canada at a price below the cost of freight and packaging in Canada. It could not have been packaged in the Okanagan Valley for the price for which it was sold there. It could not have been packaged in the Niagara Peninsula for the price at which it was sold in the Niagara Peninsula. Consequently, that fruit salad trade is totally lost to the peach, pear and other fruit producers in Canada.
Currency and Exchange Act
We must have reasonable measures because the markets from which this product came do not accept a comparable amount of fruit under any terms if it were to be shipped from Canada. There are sanitary and other artificial trade barriers that would absolutely prohibit our sale to the country of origin in this particular instance. This requires redress and the renegotiation for fair trade between ourselves and our world trading partners.
There are many small producers in Canada, particularly in the farm trade, who are unorganized and therefore cannot afford to prepare for action which is taken against us in such places as the United States. They cannot afford to prepare the evidence which is necessary to establish that there is in fact injury done to the Canadian market as a result of improperly and unfairly priced products arriving in our market.
I hope that this Bill we are debating today will at least address this in part. It does not address such circumstances as took place when the potato industry came under review in the United States. There was no viable organization that could in fact fight that case in the quasi judicial process which took place in the United States. Consequently, the potato agency in the Province of New Brunswick is absolutely strapped. There was no government assistance to protect Canadian trade and its just rights in a foreign market. These matters must be addressed. It will take several years before the potato industry in Canada can recover a viable operation as a result of the expenditures it incurred to protect the interests of the export trade in the United States. Our representations to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), have all been rejected out of hand.
Another example is the forest industry. I agree that the forest industry was able to finance itself because its group included giants that could have assumed the total expense with only a small dent to their treasury. However, when it comes to exports in the agricultural market, the Government must recognize that the total trade is the very lifeline of our financial survival. This problem should be addressed differently. I ask the Minister to give consideration to this.
The disposition of surpluses by other countries can take place in many ways. For instance, a group of agricultural processors in the United States decided that they had an excess of their product. They determined that if they sold 10 per cent of their total storage holdings at any price anywhere in the world, they would then be capable of marketing the balance at a profit and could recover any loss on the first 10 per cent of sales. This did not take place with government sponsorships but through the co-operation of the processing industry itself. There is no vehicle in this Bill, in any other legislation in the House or in other international agreements to protect an agricultural product from the efforts of a cartel to dispose of surplus. These are matters which must be given much more serious consideration. They should be addressed in this Bill.
In closing the debate, perhaps the Minister could tell us if the Bill leaves us totally without the responsibility of paying

June 26, 1984
Currency and Exchange Act
penalties or compensation to a trading partner whose trade may be perceived to be interrupted by virtue of dumping or any other exercise which this Act permits the Government to take to prohibit the trade of a particular product. According to our negotiations with GATT and our legislation, we have only applied penalties against imports subject to a compensation to be paid to the country which may consider that it was damaged because it could no longer export to Canada. There are a number of products which need attention. While we must deal with the agricultural industry in general, it is presently the wine industry that is in particularly serious trouble. We must ask for fair trade from those who would take up our market at the expense of our own producers.
The tobacco industry must be examined on somewhat the same basis. Are the imports of tobacco coming in under fair trade practices or are those imports arriving at prices which do not bear proper relationship to the cost in the country of origin? Perhaps we may have to establish some artificial trade barriers of our own and negotiate them as acceptable in order to preserve any production in the horticultural field in this country.
I implore the Minister to arrange for the acceptance of the notion that the moneys spent to subsidize exporters-not producers-from the European Economic Community will be paid instead as a subsidy to the farmer himself, because it seems that this is the only way we can impose dumping duties and penalties for the appearance of that product on our market.
There is no question that it is an invasion of what was intended in the GATT agreement. We should no longer accept an improperly established artificial subsidy. It is time to make a decision about the wine industry. I would also ask the Minister to address the problems of the tea industry. We need duties on the import of tea into Canada that are comparable to those which our industry would experience when it exports. It is necessary for the preservation of jobs in Saint-John, Montreal and the Toronto area.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: There follows a ten-minute period for questions or comments. If there are no questions, or comments, we will proceed to debate.

Mr. Speaker, first I would like to point out to the House that the report on this Bill was presented in June 1982. The emphasis was to get this Bill through so legislation could be put in place. That was 24 months ago. Now we are being asked to rush this Bill through the House. I am in favour, in general, of what has transpired. But why have we had to wait 24 months?
There are many inequities relating to the Anti-dumping Tribunal which should have been addressed a long time ago. Let me relate a difficult experience concerning one of my constituents, a Japanese Canadian who is a tool manufacturer. There has been an ongoing battle for 18 months regarding whether a certain drill is of an industrial type or a consumer
type. In spite of the fact that 93 per cent of the sales are in the consumer market, three years ago one catalogue in Japan showed that the drill was equal to an industrial tool, and this drill is now being treated as an industrial tool. That is an inequity that has not been looked at in depth. The literature is looked at, but no one takes the trouble to find out what the facts really are. The case I have outlined is a serious problem. The company set up a manufacturing facility in Canada and created 50 jobs. But because of the attitude of the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Bussieres) and the Anti-dumping Tribunal the company may move its entire operation to Georgia. When we put this type of Bill together, we must be careful not to drive more industry and equity capital out of the country. We have lost billions of dollars since 1977. I stated in the House on Friday that we lost some $40.5 billion. I think the figure is $47.8 billion of equity capital that has left Canada, and in turn Canada has had to borrow foreign capital to the extent of almost $100 billion to keep covering the deficit.
This Bill addresses subsidized exports. It addresses situations where other countries, in order to create an industrial base, do the entire financing, not only for the building but for all the equipment and the working capital. We cannot go that far but that is what we have to compete against. Let us look at what happens when we have to go to the capital markets and borrow money at current rates which at the moment for medium industries are 13.5 per cent to 14 per cent. We have to compete with zero interest rates. Now how can we do that? The United States has certain programs that provide for minimal interest rates to companies that borrow, which rates are in effect until production is at full volume. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, we have to compete against different plans in different countries. In the Bill it states that this will be taken into consideration. The words are: "Subsidies and Countervailing Duties should be taken into account by the Tribunal. Notice that the words "should be" are used. Those words should be "will be". Otherwise how do we protect Canadian industry?
The Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) mentioned hog bristles. When he talked about that I thought about the petro-chemical industry. The Chinese are probably wiser than we are. Chinese sell hog bristles at an extremely high price. Hog bristles are a raw material. This allows the Chinese to fill the hog bristle brush market with China's own manufactured products. How does this relate to the petrochemical industry? On Friday, the Minister announced a great plan to save the Canadian petro-chemical industry. He has offered to provide loans to the petro-chemical industry in order for people to convert their process from oil to natural gas and natural gas liquids. What value have loans got unless you bring down the cost of the raw material to a level competitive with other trading partners? Why not remove the taxes from natural gas and natural gas liquids in order to be competitive? But we throw money out the window when we say: "We will give loans, guarantees and grants". Why create an industry when you have a surplus of raw material? Why not bring the price of that raw material down to a level which will enable us
June 26, 1984

to compete? Why can we not use some ingenuity so we can export a finished product from one of our natural resources?
We have iron ore. The supply is diminishing at economical prices. Why should we ship iron ore out of the country at minimal cost and in turn buy steel from foreign suppliers? Perhaps we should protect the price of the base material. We have to do something to protect our industries.
I would like to address the steel industry. Dofasco is probably one of the finest steel companies in the world. Dofasco is so advanced in technology that its productivity equals that of any corporation in the entire world. Dofasco reinvests its profits and its cash in research and development. Dofasco continuously brings in Japanese engineers to the plant. People at Dofasco continuously check with other people elsewhere in the world to make certain that it has the highest level of productivity of any steel company in the world. If it is faced with competition because we have not done our job against dumping, that is wrong.
Stelco has built an entire new complex. It is probably the ultimate in new technology. The money that went into that complex was not in the form of grants, it was not in the form of interest-free loans, it was money earned and raised in debt by the corporation to bring up the standard to world-class level. We have industries at world-class level that must be protected.
About a year and a half ago several of our steel companies imported steel plate that would have hurt Algoma Steel. Algoma is a smaller corporation located in northern Ontario. It creates employment for an important part of our population. Fortunately, the Anti-dumping Tribunal jumped in and imposed a penalty on the people who imported the product. I spoke to a gentleman involved. He said: "I am delighted I have to pay that additional duty. It is wrong that I, as an importer, should be able to bring a product into Canada, similar to a product made in Canada, at distress prices."
We must also look at Finished products. I hope they will conduct an analysis of products from Pacific Rim countries and from Third World countries. Grants will be provided from Canada to some of these countries at no cost to them. If we start importing products from those countries for moneys which we have given them, again Canadian citizens will be subjected to an inequity. Not only will they face the inequity of giving money to other countries for which there is no return, but people will be driven out of work because those countries can compete and undercut our costs. This is a serious matter.
Free trade is fine, but what is free trade? No one has answered this question. I have not found an economist in Canada who can tell me what free trade is. Furthermore, economists never talk about the profits of corporations when they refer to what will happen in the economy. Free trade is no longer free because non-tariff barriers have been put in place by every country in the world. Non-tariff barriers are either subsidies or financing at zero cost. Other countries are aware of the importance of creating jobs. They are much more aware
Currency and Exchange Act
than Canada. If we were concerned about creating jobs, our trade would not have dropped to 50 per cent of Japan's trade today when we exceeded that of Japan in 1968.
We are trying to put teeth into our border. We are trying to put teeth into our duties. However, I am nervous that we do not have the expertise to analyse the costs which have been incurred by other countries. We must bring in experts from the private sector. They are the ones who will be affected. Public servants who have not manufactured a piece of steel do not know how to assess what goes into a piece of steel. Philosophically they know, but they do not know the hard facts concerning the comparison of products.
What about the Pony? A great many of them are coming into Canada from Korea. I should like to know the costing which permits the sale of a product in this country at about 30 per cent less than we can produce it. My friends to the left will say that it is because large bonuses were paid to executives of automobile manufacturers. That would not add a dollar per car. I do not agree with the executives taking those funds. It was greed on their part and it was the wrong time to do it. However, how do we know the true costs involved in the manufacture of those vehicles?
Let us look at what happened just recently in terms of our lumber exports to the United States. In effect, the Americans were extremely fair to us at the time. There had been a great deal of subsidization of the lumber industry to upgrade its facilities so that our productivity level would be higher than that of others. The Americans were right in looking at it but they were fair to us. They are our biggest trading partner and we must protect that. We must look at the products of other countries which are coming into Canada on an equal basis, as they look at ours. We should not attack Canada, we should defend it.
I was concerned as a result of committee consideration that the Tariff Board was to be empowered to review decisions made by the Anti-dumping Tribunal. However, that was not permitted. Interested parties may make representations, but we wanted someone else in there as a doublecheck. We do not have checks and balances in this country. We need a doublecheck to ensure that the system is equitable both to consumers and to manufacturers. Let us not only think of consumers. Manufacturers create jobs. When there are two million people unemployed in the country, that is our major concern. Possibly that is the reason this Bill sat for two years in the Department and nothing was done about it. Perhaps it was because unemployment levels had not reached the critical level of today.
In terms of the capital goods sector, we recommended further study of the innate problems of that sector. A little was done but not enough. Why are we not the major manufacturers of mining equipment? We were very progressive in mining in the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s. We used to produce a great deal of the mining equipment required in Canada. Now we import more than we produce.
Also we recommended that the role of current import agencies be examined in relation to one another. This was not acted upon. We should review the agencies importing these

June 26, 1984
products. We should review the deals in which they are involved under the table. We should review state to state deals which are being made. We must review products from steel mills in Japan, for example, which came into the country from Houston. This pipe was going into Houston and filtering through to Calgary at a cost which was a third less than the price for which Phoenix Tube could make it in Saskatoon.
Whether the Tribunal will catch up with all the slips in the market is a big question, but we must at least start. This Bill is nothing but a start. It should be reviewed by the Finance Committee at least every six months because of the tricks which are being pulled on us and because the possibility of creating pure fair trade in the world is important.
These are difficult times for Canadians. These are difficult times for unemployed Canadians. This Bill could have a direct impact upon many lives in the country. This Bill could assist Canada, but it would be only one spoke in the wheel. It could help Canada to get from its pathetic trading position now back to its trading position of 1968. We must put an economic policy in place which will bring out the entrepreneurial spirit. If we do, at least it would be in place to protect Canadian citizens who undertook risks and created jobs. We must be careful that the Bill is not directed against our major trading partners, those who buy a great deal from us. We must ensure that the Bill only addresses those countries which are unfair or are not dealing with us in an equitable way. Hopefully, in the future the words "free trade" will become meaningful.
It being two o'clock, the House will now proceed to statements by Members pursuant to Standing Order 21.

subsubtopic: EFFECT OF GOVERNMENT POLICY ON FARMERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to express the hurt, frustration, and anger of many thousands of family farmers at the boast of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) that Canadians now pay 12 per cent of their disposal income for food as compared to 16 per cent when the present Liberal Party came to power. As a result of the Liberal cheap food policy, Canada has lost tens of thousands of family farmers. Their net incomes have dropped dramatically. Over 50 per cent of our family farmers must work off the farm in order to sustain their families and to remain on the land.
The Liberal Party's cheap food policy benefits consumers in the short run, but when the Liberals have destroyed the family farmer, consumers will pay, pay, pay. It need not happen.

subtopic: SWEARING IN OF NEW CABINET-CLOSED TO TELEVISION CAMERAS
SWEARING IN OF NEW CABINET-CLOSED TO TELEVISION CAMERAS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, by barring the media from Saturday's swearing in ceremony of the new Cabinet, Canada's new temporary Prime Minister has given the Canadian people a clear indication that the Liberal Party has not changed one iota in form or substance.
Closed door swearing in ceremonies are a throwback to yesterday, from whence the temporary Prime Minister comes. What is so secret about a swearing in ceremony? The temporary Prime Minister replies: "I thought I would do it in a business like way." That may be the way the temporary Prime Minister did business yesterday as a director of CPR, but it will not wash on Main Street.
It is obvious that the real reason the temporary Prime Minister wants a closed door meeting is because there is no real change. The Ministers of Transport, Treasury Board, Labour and International Trade, who brought Canada high record interest rates, unemployment, and bankruptcies, are still running the store, and the temporary Prime Minister has not changed a thing. As the Minister of Energy can testify, the same backroom gang are in charge. Nothing has changed. The temporary Prime Minister just wants to hide it from the Canadian people.

subtopic: OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED PACIFIC FISHERY LEGISLATION
OPPOSITION TO PROPOSED PACIFIC FISHERY LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this morning I received a telegram from the Mayor of Ucluelet, a community in my riding which is dependent upon the fishing industry and tourism. He asked me, on behalf of the community, to do everything I can to stop the proposed Pacific salmon fisheries legislation from passing before his community and others have an opportunity to assess the impact. It is clear to Mayor Larson, and it is clear to me, that the impact will be devastating. The proposals outlined in the draft legislation to restructure the Pacific fishery would wreak havoc on the West Coast. Coastal communities sense this, and so do fishermen. Yesterday some 1,500 fishermen tied up their boats in Port Alberni as a demonstration against the Government's proposals and its inability to manage the West Coast fishery.
Fishermen, coastal communities, native leaders, and all others in B.C. who are concerned about the future of our salmon stocks, are angry that the Government's proposals do not address in any substantial way any measures to increase salmon stocks. This proposed legislation does little more than ensure the financial ruin of fishermen.
If the Government continues with its present approach, it will lead not only to the gutting of the commercial fleet and the loss of thousands of jobs, but it will also lead to the eventual closure of the sports fishery and have serious impact
June 26, 1984

on the native food fishery. Many coastal communities may not be able to survive. If the Government is serious about conservation and restoration of our salmon stocks, it should introduce buy-back legislation which is acceptable to most, and allow the rest of its proposals adequate scrutiny, as is being demanded.

subtopic: SCHEDULED VISIT OF HIS HOLINESS THE POPE TO FORT SIMPSON, N.W.T.
SCHEDULED VISIT OF HIS HOLINESS THE POPE TO FORT SIMPSON, N.W.T.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government of Canada has invited His Holiness the Pope to make a state visit to Fort Simpson, Northwest Territories. Fort Simpson is a village with a population of less than 1,000. It may well experience an influx of up to 50,000 souls at that time. The planning committee estimates local expenses, not otherwise covered, will amount to about half a million dollars. Obviously Fort Simpson is unable to come up with this large amount of money, and such expenses should be borne by Canada.
The Department of External Affairs will not pay and says it is the responsibility of Indian Affairs. Indian Affairs will not pay and says it is the responsibility of External Affairs or of the Canadian Council of Catholic Bishops. Everyone is passing the buck. The situation is getting desperate. If the Government cannot decide which Department is to provide the funds, the Papal visit to Fort Simpson may well end in a fiasco.

subtopic: STATE OF INDUSTRY-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
STATE OF INDUSTRY-CALL FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, for the past several months the Members in this House have heard the Government pumping itself up for the wonderful state of the economy. Perhaps these same people would care to tell us why a shocking 50 per cent of Canadians do not take an annual vacation. I doubt that half of the families in this country forgo a holiday by choice. More likely, they cannot afford to travel during their leisure time. The Government has dealt Canadians a real double whammy. On the one hand it has taken away the right of Canadians to enjoy vacations. On the other hand it has crippled our tourist industry without batting an eye.
Ten years ago Canada enjoyed 4.2 per cent of the international travel market. Now, due chiefly to government waffling and languid lip service, our share has plummeted to 2.6 per cent. The Government is hurting itself. It appears to be bending over backwards to slap its own behind. Instead, it should be hard selling Canadian vacations to the people who live here. The systems are already in place to accommodate vacationing Canadians. The only road block is the Government itself.

Mr. Speaker, I was disturbed to learn this weekend that the Liberal Government is toying with the notion of a flat tax that would tax every Canadian taxpayer at the same rate, regardless of income. In considering the flat tax proposal the Government has to share the stage with such notables as the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Evans), and Peter Pocklington, one of the more outrageous contenders for the Tory leadership last year.
It is not hard to tell what a flat tax would do to Canada. It would attack what little fairness there is in our tax system by taking more tax from the poor and taking less tax from the rich. Even that ultra right wing think tank on the West Coast admits that.
At a flat rate of a little more than 19 per cent, people who earn between $5,000 and $15,000 a year would pay on average $176 more in income tax. Those Canadians who make more than $200,000 would pay $37,000 less in income tax. It should not surprise anyone that the people who would be hardest hit by this notion would be the elderly poor because they have little chance of increasing their income in the future and taking advantage of the tax saving that goes with it.
Proponents believe a flat income tax rate is good because it would leave money in the hands of the rich and they know what to do with that money to stimulate the economy. That sounds like a pretty thin excuse for a major tax grab on behalf of Canada's richest citizens. The notion of a flat earth was relegated to the trash bin of history centuries ago. The flat tax proposal deserves nothing less than the same fate.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (St. John's West):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is directed to the despairing Minister of Finance who can do nothing. The Minister met Mr. Turner yesterday and apparently gave him new economic forecasts. Will he tell the House what are those economic forecasts, and will he make an economic statement in this House, give the House new economic forecasts and a plan of action before we adjourn on June 29, or will he continue his "do nothing" attitude of despair that dooms the people of Canada to unemployment and lack of economic growth?

Mr. Speaker, far from a "do nothing approach", this Government has been very active in terms of attempting to promote growth and in terms of ensuring that interest rates will remain as low as possible. For instance, I would remind my hon. friend that, on the basis of the growth of the economy in the first quarter, the projected growth for this year would still be 4.4 per cent-
3.2 per cent.

It is 4.4 per cent on a year over year basis. I would invite my hon. friend to look at that.
As far as interest rates are concerned, I would tell my hon. friend that in Canada we have a policy which has succeeded in achieving a lower rate of interest than that of the United States. That is a record which was not achieved in the short
period when the Hon. Member was the Minister of Finance. I am sure it will not be achieved as long as the Hon. Member contradicts his own Leader on what they should do with interest rates.
With respect to the last point raised by the Hon. Member, I did not provide Mr. Turner with forecasts yesterday.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to the Minister of Finance. I would remind him that he should not be so very pleased with the performance in Canada. It was 3.2 per cent against 9.7 per cent for the comparable period in the United States. That is performance?
The only action with which the Minister has responded against the weak dollar is a short-term policy which will prop up the dollar with high interest rates. I would remind him that it is not a short-term problem. It is a problem which has been going on since 1977 when our dollar was $1.03. It is now 76 cents. I would ask the Minister, in face of this and in face of the need for a long-term recovery program which would re-establish strength in the Canadian economy and would give fundamental strength to the Canadian dollar, when will he bring in a policy of long-term growth and not just short-term propping up?

Mr. Speaker, if the Hon. Member wants to compare figures with the United States he will have to accept the Figure of 4.4 per cent which I have mentioned. I would invite him to check his facts and consult his advisers in that regard.
As to the issue of providing long-term policies and long-term approaches-indeed, medium and long-term-that was the basic approach contained in the last two Budgets. They have produced good results for the Canadian economy, and are continuing to produce good results. We are not going to put ourselves into the situation of inventing short cuts which will damage the Canadian economy. We have adopted medium and long-term measures which are producing results.
At the same time we have taken steps to help those most in need in this country, whether it was the $50 increase of GIS which was recently approved by the House, whether it was the $4.8 billion worth of incentives contained in the recovery program and which is being spent at the present time, or whether it is the billions of dollars being spent in the Department of Employment and Immigration for training and direct job-creation. This Government has put forward a combination of short-term, medium-term, and long-term measures to ensure that the economy will be able to compete with the rest of the world and will be one of the most efficient economies in the industrial world. That is what we are working toward. That is what we are achieving. I recognize that it will take longer than I wish, and longer than the Hon. Member wishes. But, indeed, we are working on the basis of medium and long-term measures which will be helpful to our economy.
June 26, 1984

Mr. Speaker, the Minister is making my point for me. Canadians have been waiting for 20 years for performance from this Government. We have seen the result of this in an 11.7 per cent unemployment rate, against 7.5 per cent in the United States, and a growth rate in the economy in the first quarter of this year of 9.7 per cent in the U.S. against 3.2 per cent in Canada. We must do better.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to return to the subject of the Canadian dollar. Canadians are seeing the cost of the low dollar in their food, vacations, cars which they buy from abroad, clothing, television sets, gasoline, and virtually everything. The cost of financing the Government's borrowing overseas has increased over $1 billion as a result of the recent decline in the dollar. Does the Minister regard the current exchange crisis with a sense of urgency? Is he determined to bring in policies which will attack the situation, or are we going to see a long drift through this summer in which nothing will happen and the dollar will go as low as 70 cents or 75 cents?

Mr. Speaker, I refuse to talk about an exchange crisis. As I have mentioned, the Canadian dollar has gone down vis-a-vis the U.S. dollar at the same level as the German Deutschmark. It has gone down less than the currencies of all the other main industrial countries, whether it be Britain, Switzerland, France or Japan. If the Hon. Member would look over a longer period he would find that the Canadian dollar, rather than falling against those other currencies, has increased in value against those currencies in the last year or two.
One of the problems which many exporters have mentioned to me was the difficulty they had in penetrating European and other markets where they were in competition with European and Japanese products because the Canadian dollar was relatively strong against those currencies. They had great difficulty penetrating those markets because the Canadian dollar was stronger than those of other countries, both in their domestic markets and in their export markets. The Hon. Member should bear that in mind. He should not only consider the relationship between the Canadian dollar and the U.S. dollar, but the relationship between the Canadian dollar and all the other currencies. If he looks at other currencies he will find that indeed the Canadian dollar has gained strength over the last several years.
As far as the comment of waiting for 20 years is concerned, my hon. friend should know that during the last 16 years this country has created more jobs proportionately than any other industrialized country. That is what we have done. This country has known, as an average, a higher rate of growth than the other industrialized countries, except Japan, over the last 16 years. This is what has happened in this country during that period. Rather than disparaging this record we should, as a country, be proud when one looks objectively at what has been done here.

And that has not been done by constantly moaning and complaining.

subsubtopic: LOCATION OF ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BRANCH IN MONTREAL
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport. Can the Minister explain the rationale behind establishing the accident investigation operation of the Canadian Aviation Safety Board in Montreal, since it will involve the transfer of more than 50 senior people, considerable inconvenience, heavy costs, and unnecessary disruption? Additionally, it will affect the ability of accident investigators to co-ordinate their work with other government agencies such as Transport Canada, the National Research Council, the Aviation Safety Bureau, and many others?

subsubtopic: LOCATION OF ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BRANCH IN MONTREAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very surprised at the Hon. Member's question, coming as he does from a part of the country in which there is always an interest in making sure that there is a fair and equitable distribution of federal government activity. The Government is committed to the basic principle that the entire country should be able to support and secure federal activity, offices, and operations. I gather from the Hon. Member's question that
that is not a principle endorsed by the Conservative Party. That is one reason why they are on the opposition benches.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: LOCATION OF ACCIDENT INVESTIGATION BRANCH IN MONTREAL
speechtext: Until the next election.

Mr. Speaker, we are quite in tune with decentralization when it makes some sense. Since the news which I just spoke of came out, three senior investigators have taken early retirement, two senior analysts have taken lateral moves, more personnel are considering similar options, and morale is low in the Department. Will the Minister agree that this will impair, rather than enhance, air safety in Canada?

Mr. Speaker, quite to the contrary. I would say that it will substantially fulfil the basic objective which we put forward in establishing the Canadian Aviation Safety Board. It was to be a board quite separate and independent from the ongoing functions of the Department of Transport. The original purpose of the safety board was to divorce the investigation inquiry of accidents from the standard setting and review functions of the Department. One of the ways to ensure that that would happen would be to separate them in a geographical as well as a functional way.
I can think of no better location than the City of Montreal, which is very much the centre of aviation development for Canada. It is the head of the international aviation agencies. It is the area where we have our major airline centres and our major maintenance bases. Both logic and justification show that the placement of the aviation safety bureau in Montreal is a decision which will enable that board to fulfil its functions most appropriately and accurately.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member will know that we have received many representations from the Ontario Wine Council clearly indicating that there is what they consider massive dumping or subsidization of wines coming into Canada from the European Common Market. Member's thoughts on this situation and whether he feels the Bill goes anywhere toward helping the Ontario wine industry.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) for bringing up this very important point. I hope the Bill does address that problem. This year Ontario wine growers have sold 20 per cent less than during the same period in the previous year. It is not only one product; there are so many other things being dumped in Canada, wine being but one example.
The wine industry in Ontario is very important. I am not convinced that our method of taxation of wine is done equitably. In such countries as France and Italy you can buy what is commonly referred to as vin ordinaire at a very nominal price, a little less than you would pay for a Coca-Cola. When good French wine comes into the country we tax it very heavily, but what is happening is this. The French and Italians used to have control of the whole market, but many other countries have now infringed upon this exclusive market which France and Italy controlled for a long time. People like the Ontario wine growers are producing a wine that is palatable to the Canadian palate, and to the American. Therefore, in order to compete the French and Italian wine industry have been subsidized so as to dispose of their product, since they cannot afford to store any more than they have already. Thus, they are dumping it in Canada.
We have to look carefully at the Bill. As I said earlier, there is a weakness. I believe it will take experts from the wine
June 26, 1984

industry to assess the damage being done, as opposed to public servants or people appointed by Liberals to this board. I am really concerned because in the Niagara Belt there are 24,000 acres of vineyards and 16,000 full-time and seasonal jobs. For each of these jobs there are indirect ones. The multiplier effect takes over. I have great apprehension about the Bill accomplishing everything anticipated, but it must be adjusted to protect an industry which is so critical to southern Ontario.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there any further questions or comments? For debate, the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor).

Mr. Speaker, I want to deal with at least four principles involved in the Bill. The first one concerns the beef industry. The other day the Hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) did not seem to take seriously the fact that the beef industry in Canada, certainly in western Canada, was being ruined by the dumping of beef into the country. I take great exception to that. This industry has been very profitable for Canada. It is one of our mainstays. Now, because the European market has subsidized its industry to the point where it has piled up food, that product is dumped in Canada below the cost of production. Some people may say that that is very nice for consumers, but it is not because it means the cattle industry will be ruined. It will take years for the industry to recover, if at all. I deplore the attitude of the Government in not taking action immediately to deal with the dumping of beef in Canada. It is a serious matter and it hurts one of our industries.
My second point concerns the importation of natural products from the United States. The principle is that when no tariff has been established, someone somewhere decides what tariff the product will carry. I am referring in particular to a natural product used in the preparation of a pollutant. It came into Canada for a long time without any duty or tariff. Suddenly out of the blue there was a tariff change which demanded that importers pay a 15 per cent duty on all such imported products. A sudden change such as this forces small companies out of business. If there is to be a change in tariff, surely companies should be notified. The Department should not wait until these companies have gone to a lot of work organizing their affairs. In the case of a small company involved in the importation of this natural product, it had to prepare labels both in imperial and metric, as well as in French and English. It went to a lot of expense on the understanding that the importation of the product was duty free. Suddenly it was stuck with a 15 per cent tariff which it was told it had to pay. Certainly it hurt this small company very much.
The tariff which was used was the one on materials of all kinds used in producing or manufacturing products under heading 93811 when imported exclusively for such use or whether or not otherwise enumerated in Schedule A. It definitely showed 85001.1 as being free not only for the most favoured nation but also from the general tariff and throughout. Then a 15 per cent tariff was imposed. It is pretty serious when such a company is left in a precarious position.
Currency and Exchange Act
Approximately a year and a half later I received a letter from the Minister which indicated that to date a tariff item for the goods in question had not been introduced into the Customs Tariff. The Department floundered around for a year and a half using this tariff and that tariff. At the same time it extracted money from the business and ruined it. At the end of that period of time the Department indicated that it had not yet introduced a tariff. If that is the case, why was it not continued on the pre-tariff which was used when the business was started? This type of action does great harm. Surely the Department should not endeavour to put small companies out of business. That is what a sudden change in tariff does. It did not make up its mind as to what was the tariff. It certainly hurt small businesses but it also hurts any business in Canada. It is not much credit to the Department. It indicates that the Department does not know what it is doing.
Another area of the Bill to which I would like to refer is the one dealing with the importation of dental supplies. A dentist in my constituency ordered dental supplies by mail from the United States. He included the full postage in both directions. The dental supplies arrived in Calgary. Recently he received a telephone call from the customs office saying that duties were due on the goods. The dentist asked how much the duties were. The official told him that he could not tell him over the telephone but that the declared value of the goods was $111.25. Also the dentist was told that he had to come into the customs office himself, that he could not send anyone else. In other words, the dentist had to close his office, inconvenience all his patients slated for that day, drive at least 35 miles there and 35 miles back. What for? Customs seems to be completely inflexible. It does not seem to realize that it is there to serve the public. Also he was told to bring in his invoice when he attended at its office. He said that he did not have an invoice because it was attached to the goods. The officials told him that he had to bring an invoice with him. From where would he get an invoice since his order was made by mail? It was attached to the goods. This type of nonsense on the part of customs officials should be stopped. It is hurting business across the country. How many businesses have folded due to ridiculous attitudes such as this on the part of customs officials? They seem to think they are so powerful that they can do anything they like. Apparently they are getting away with it.
I hope the Minister will deal with this case, not just tap officials on the fingers. The invoice was attached to the dental supplies. The doctor should have been able to obtain them without wasting his time by going to the office himself. They should have been able to tell him over the telephone how much the duties were. It was nonsense to give the declared value but refuse to give the amount of duty. This type of inconvenience should not be taking place.
The next item with which I would like to deal concerns another beef or grievance I have with the Department. For many years the American Quarter Horse Association has come to Canada to take part in equestrian competitions. Many Canadian horsemen went to the United States to do likewise.

June 26, 1984
Currency and Exchange Act
Suddenly in 1983 there was a change and the Department indicated that they would have to pay 16.7 per cent on their saddles and all equipment on their competing horses. That was unheard of before. Equestrian competitors, both American and Canadian, have been crossing back and forth across the border without any duties. Suddenly someone had the idea that they would have to pay. They were not bringing in this equipment to sell. It was to be used in competition. It is a reputable organization, but it was told that it had to pay a duty on the equipment. It is a ridiculous situation.
We got in touch with the Department. The Department said they must make a deposit of several hundred dollars in order to be able to compete in Canada. When these people come to Canada they spend money. When these people come here they use hotels, buy food and purchase gifts to take back home. They spend money here. The Minister does not seem to realize that. He says they have to make a deposit. The rule reads:
Animals and equipment for use therewith for pasturage, competition, training or breeding.
That is free. That is what it states in the regulations. Why is authority given to someone at the border and somebody in the customs tariff office to force these people to pay or leave a deposit when they are just coming here to take part in a competition? They are not coming from Russia. They do not have to escape from the United States; they are coming here to take part in a competition. They will leave money here, something that is good for the country, yet we have this type of behaviour. A clean-up is required in many of these areas.
The last point I want to raise in this connection is a very serious problem. It involves farm machinery. Under the tariff rules, farm machinery should come in free. Somehow or other the Department has decided that if your farm equipment breaks down and you require a replacement part, you have to pay duty on that replacement part. Farm machinery wears out. Parts will be required.
Let me talk about the 1600 Ford Easy-Rider air-flow self-propelled fertilizer, a machine used for fertilizing. That is straight farm use to increase production in this country. Under the tariff it comes in free. The self-propelled fertilizer spreaders manufactured by Lor-Al Corporation, complete with fertilizer, spreader and applicator incorporated therein, comes in free under the respective tariff.
An accident occurred. The chassis was destroyed. The fertilizer equipment was fine. They were told they would have to pay duty on the replacement chassis. This chassis is not used on any other farm machinery. It is not used off the farm. Only 50 were manufactured in the United States for Lor-Al specifically for the 1,600 Easy-Rider air-flow self-propelled fertilizer. Only 50 were made. One was ordered. They were told they would have to pay duty on it, as if it were part of a car or truck. This is farm machinery.
I appreciate the attitude of the Deputy Minister and his chief assistant. They say that this is now being reviewed so that all farm equipment with a chassis will no longer have the
chassis come in duty free. There will be a tariff. It is a new classification. It is supposed to start this year. I take serious objection to that. When the House of Commons set out that farm equipment coming into Canada for use on the farm to increase our production would enter free, the public servants or bureaucrats should not change that and say that duties and tariffs will apply to replacement parts. It does not make sense.
A chassis for the 1600 Ford Easy-Rider air-flow self-propelled fertilizer is a specially made chassis. It is for that machine only. No one will buy it for anything else. It is now said that every machine with a chassis will not come in duty free whether it is for agriculture, working on the highway or working in the mountains. There will now be a tariff fee. That is completely contrary to what the Members of the House of Commons said when they said that all farm machinery coming into Canada to produce food cheaper and help agriculture, our basic primary industry, should enter free. Now it is being changed, not by leaps and bounds but by inches at a time. First the chassis will be taxed, then the pistons, and so on. It does not make sense.
I wish to bring these cases to the attention of the House of Commons and the Minister. Every case I mention affects a number of people across this country who are dissatisfied and unhappy. It is hurting farming and small business. It is time that we in this country help to keep our small businesses and farmers in a fluid position so that they can continue to operate rather than go into bankruptcy.
The next point I want to mention is with regard to the importation of clay. Many people in this country do clay modelling, producing beautiful vases and other items. Clay had been coming into Canada duty free. In some parts of Canada it now enters duty free and in other parts of Canada duty must be paid. That is not right. This was brought to the attention of the officials. They are still quarrelling about it.
Truckloads of this clay come into Alberta and British Columbia. It depends on which port it enters as to whether it is charged duty. This is to be used to produce in this country. It is necessary for the manufacture of the pottery in that industry and it should enter duty free. It should not be taxed. If there is going to be a tax on any of these items, it should not be so great that it drives small businesses out of business.
Any equipment brought into this country to help us produce for farm purposes should not be taxed whether it comes in in whole or in part. There is no rhyme or reason to put a tax on the chassis of a 1600 Ford Easy-Rider air-flow self-propelled fertilizer. It is a farm machine and should not be taxed. I emphasize that over and over again. Once we tax the chassis on this machine, we will inch by inch get to the point where we tax everything used in the production of food in this country. That would be a disaster.
