speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have this opportunity today to speak to Bill C-49, the Western Arctic (Inuvialuit) Claims Settlement Act.

June 26, 1984
Western Arctic Agreement
Hon. Members are probably aware that the purpose of this Act is to legalize the claims settlement concluded with the Committee for Original Peoples' Entitlement which defends the interests of the Western Arctic Inuvialuit. Mr. Speaker, it is a historic measure, since it enshrines the first comprehensive settlement of this kind concluded with a native group in Canada's North. This Bill shows us what the future has in store. We hope we shall soon see the day when similar settlements will occur throughout the North and native claims in the Yukon and the Northwest Territories will have been settled in a definitive and satisfactory manner.
For some time now, the settlement of outstanding native claims has been a decisive factor in developing Canada's regions north of 60.
Certain aspects of the economic, political and social situation that has prevailed in the North for many years are a source of profound concern. After the rate of economic expansion slowed down, the people of the North, instead of trying to plan the future together, were often paralyzed by bitter disputes about development, the environment and other issues. Mr. Speaker, in these conditions it was important for the federal Government to choose a plan of action that would put stability and co-operation in the place of uncertainty and discord, a plan that would encourage the people of the North to become more active participants in planning the future of their territory; a plan that would involve the native peoples of the North in decision-making on political and economic issues. However, native claims must be settled satisfactorily before this plan can be expected to show any results.
As long as the problem of native claims is not resolved, distrust and resentment will prevent parties from co-operating and making the concessions that are a pre-requisite for developing a plan of action for development of the North. Settlement of the claims is a key element in our plans for the North.
Hon. Members will recall that more funds have been earmarked for research and negotiations. We have made it clear to the native groups concerned that the federal Government was very serious and sincere in its desire to negotiate a fair settlement for outstanding claims as soon as possible. Despite the complexity of this type of comprehensive negotiations, real progress has been achieved. Furthermore, the agreement in principle with respect to the claims of the Council of Yukon Indians was recently accepted by negotiators for both parties, by the Government of Yukon and by the federal cabinet. Now the agreement only has to be ratified by the Yukon Indians.
As for the claims of the Dene Association and the Metis, which represent the main native groups in the MacKenzie Valley, and those of the Tungavik Federation of the Nunavut, on behalf of the Eastern Arctic Inuit, negotiations are proceeding satisfactorily. Since we started making tangible progress
on the claims issue, there has been a considerable change in atmosphere in the Territories, both in relations between the North and Ottawa and within the Territories. Distrust and intransigence have made way for mutual trust, co-operation and a willingness to make concessions. The people of the North, including the native peoples, are once again prepared to work together with the federal Government and define and set priorities for the future.
We shall therefore continue to pressure for progress in settling comprehensive claims in the North. During the next ten years, we shall see a new upsurge in economic development in the North, in the mining and oil industry as well as in other sectors. Economic growth will be largely stimulated by improving economic and political conditions which will stabilize as a result of substantial progress in claims settlements.
I shall now, if I may, return to the legislation before the House. This Bill concerns claims presented by the Inuvialuit.
These are some 2,500 Inuvialuit living in six communities in the Northwest Territories, along the coast of the Beaufort Sea and on the islands off the coast. The territory they have always inhabited is immense, covering nearly 435,000 square kilometers of land and sea. The Inuvialuit who have lived there for centuries, depend on hunting and fishing for their livelihood.
Mr. Speaker, it was not easy to negotiate a comprehensive settlement. The Committee for Original Peoples' Entitlement presented its claim seven years ago to the federal Government. This agreement demonstrates the sincerity and determination with which all parties have worked towards a definitive solution that would be fair to the Inuvialuit, the people of the North and all Canadians. Comprehensive claims are not concerned exclusively with land, although environmental planning is a very considerable factor in negotiations. Comprehensive claims are based on the principles of ancestral rights, in other words the historic claims of a population that has lived for centuries within a certain territory on which it depends for its livelihood and whose cultural and economic survival depends on the future use and development of that territory.
Through these comprehensive negotiations, we have tried to conclude an agreement that:
Preserves Inuvialuit cultural identity and values within a changing northern society;
Guarantees the equality of the Inuvialuit and enables them to be meaningful participants in the northern and national economy and society;
Protects and preserves the Arctic wildlife, environment and ecosystems.
This agreement which will be implemented through this act is basically an agreement under which Canada will grant to the Inuvialuit certain rights, privileges and benefits with a view to achieving the objectives already mentioned. In exchange, the Inuvialuit agree to relinquish any title on certain
June 26, 1984

lands in the Northwest Territories and the Yukon as well as on certain adjacent offshore islands.
The agreement we have concluded deals basically with three major issues: the land and its use, the provisions related to economic expansion, social progress and compensation, and finally wildlife and environment.
With respect to the land, the Inuvialuit will receive titles to approximately 91,000 square kilometres of land within the
435.000	square kilometre area they traditionally occupied. They will own both surface and subsurface rights to almost
11.000	square kilometres of land adjacent to the six main communities. They will also receive title to a further 78,000 square kilometres, with full surface rights and subsurface rights to sand and gravel, but not to oil, gas or minerals. Approximately 2,000 square kilometres of land in the Cape Bathurst area will also be held as a protected, non-development area.
Among the economic and social benefits provided under the agreement, they will receive $45 million, in 1977 dollars-the year they filed their claims-to be paid directly in a series of payments to be made annually until 1997. There will also be an Economic Enhancement Fund of $10 million to help the Inuvialuit participate fully in the Western Arctic economy, and a Social Development Fund of $7.5 million to help the Inuvialuit solve the problems which accompany social transition.
The agreement grants the Inuvialuit certain preferential and exclusive rights to harvest wildlife in the settlement region. The agreement also provides assistance in integrating the Inuvialuit into the decision-making process involving wildlife management within their territories.
Mr. Speaker, the provisions of this agreement will give the results which the Inuvialuit and the federal Government are seeking. It will enable that group of native people to maintain their ancestral way of life and go on with their traditional activities.
Thanks to the Economic Enhancement Fund and the Social Development Fund, the Inuvialuit will play a greater role in the economic growth of the North, and they will also have their say in setting their own social and economic priorities.
The agreement was concluded earlier this year by teams of negotiators representing COPE and the federal Government. I might add that the Governments of the Northwest Territories and the Yukon as well as the federal Cabinet gave their agreement.
The Yukon Indian Council, the Nunavut Tungavik Federation as well as the Dene and Metis of the Northwest Territories have signed bilateral agreements to settle the problems created by the redistribution of their interests in the lands described in the agreement.
Western Arctic Agreement
Last month, when the Inuvialuit voted to ratify the agreement, the overwhelming majority-81 per cent-was in favour. The only thing left to do, Mr. Speaker, is for Parliament to adopt this Bill so that the agreement be implemented. We hope Hon. Members will consider this Bill quickly and agree to its adoption.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I get into my presentation, I would like to inform the Parliamentary Secretary that when the Bill goes before the Committee of the Whole it is my intention to ask several questions. I hope there is expert advice available to him at that time so that committee stage might be dealt with expeditiously.
I was rather disappointed, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) has not seen fit to appear in the House this afternoon on this issue. It may be that he is still pondering his political future after the events of the weekend before last. However, I would have liked to hear from the Minister personally with respect to Bill C-49. It is also disillusioning, Sir, when we have to wait for several minutes before we get two Ministers of the Crown sitting in their seats so that the motion for second reading could be properly moved and seconded. I guess it just goes to show the importance which the Government attaches to these issues.
When we consider the COPE agreement and the resolutions of various outstanding comprehensive land claims, Sir, we know that it is an agonizingly slow process. I am disappointed with the rate of progress which has been made over the last five years or six years in particular. When the present Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development took on his responsibilities in 1980, he put out a press release wherein he said he was going to resolve these outstanding land claims in a

June 26, 1984
Western Arctic Agreement
matter of six months. So far to date, since he has been in that portfolio, this is the first claim which has reached the point of resolution. And there are many more yet to come.
I do not know why this is so, Sir, but I can guess at several reasons. It might be inherent difficulties involved in the negotiation of land claims. It might, however, be deliberate stalling on the part of the Government. Alternatively, it might be ministerial incompetence. I will leave it for others to make that determination.
However, we have the COPE agreement before us now and we find ourselves in the position that it is virtually a fait accompli. We have the agreement before us today which has been ratified by the Cabinet, agreed to by the Government, and which has been ratified by a substantial 80 per cent majority of the Inuvialuit. Whatever we do with it in this House at the present time, we are unable to alter it in any substantial way, or in any way whatsoever, as far as I can determine. Therefore, it falls upon us to allow the passage of Bill C-49 without undue delay and that is the course of action which we on this side propose to undertake.
I want to say a few words about the public perception of this agreement in the area involved, the western part of the Northwest Territories, in the Delta area. The agreement is generally regarded by everyone as something which is second or third best. Most people would have liked something else but I suppose they can live with this if they really have to. That is the type of attitude which people have about it.
They are also tired of talking about it. Negotiations have gone on for so many years and caused so many dissensions that what we have now is what might be called "an agreement by attrition". People are so tired of talking of it, going into it, renegotiating it and then going back again, that they more or less are ready to accept anything that is put before them. It is not the first time I have seen this happen with the present Government.
There are some things to be said in favour of the Inuvialuit settlement. In my personal opinion, I feel it is better than the James Bay settlement. It is still a lengthy document but it is a little easier to read than the James Bay settlement. It is complex but not as complex. The provisions in it tend to be a little more specific. I believe we will have some problems with interpretation in the years to come but I do not feel the problems of interpretation will be as bad as those experienced with the James Bay agreement. The Inuvialuit settlement agreement does not envisage further legislation which will have to be passed several years hence.
You will recall, Sir, the passage just a few days ago of the Cree-Naskapi Act which was something contemplated within the James Bay agreement but which took some additional eight years to negotiate. In the meantime things were left up in the air. That situation is not contemplated in the Inuvialuit agreement, although it might arise. That is something we cannot tell at the present time.
I believe that the negotiating process ran into many difficulties because of the secrecy involved. The Government insisted
that virtually everything be done behind closed doors. It did not want the general public in on it. It chose the people with whom it wanted to negotiate, kept everyone else out of the negotiations and would not tell them what was going on. I do not believe this is the right approach. The public somehow always finds out in the end what is going on and what is going to affect them. The process in my opinion, should be open so that mistakes do not occur, or so that they can be nipped in the bud.
I will give you, Sir, some examples of avoidable mistakes which happened during the COPE negotiations. First of all, going back to the time of the agreement in principle, way back in 1978, there was the question of sand and gravel. As you are probably aware, Mr. Speaker, sand and gravel is most important in an area of permafrost. When one is doing civil work such as constructing roads in a municipality, one cannot use cut and fill techniques. It is all fill. One must dump four feet or five feet of gravel on top of the permafrost in order to preserve the frozen nature of it. Therefore, sand and gravel is very important.
Under the original agreement, the municipalities found themselves without access to sand and gravel. Had we not had that secretive process, that mistake would not have been made and we would not have beaten our heads together for months on end over a question of sand and gravel, a question which could have easily been resolved during the course of the negotiations. Subsequently we had the problem with the overlap in the Aklavik area, the overlap between the Inuvialuit claim and the Dene-Metis claim where two sets of people have traditionally used the same area. That would not have happened had the negotiations, or the partial result thereof, been made public as we went along. Instead, once people found out what was proposed to be written into the final agreement, everything blew up in the air because this matter had not been properly considered and those other people with a very real interest in that area of land had not been brought into the negotiating picture.
Another very good example of this is the 10 per cent differential which I understand was put in expressly at the request of the federal negotiator. I understand that other people involved in the secret process told him that if he did that, all hell is going to break loose. He would not believe them and that is precisely what happened when people found out what was to be in the so-called final agreement. All that could have been avoided had the Government undertaken negotiations in a proper open manner rather than trying to keep everything secret. The issues to which I referred have now been resolved, but they need not have arisen in the first place.
This Government's penchant for secrecy extended even after the final agreement had been initialled. Even though the other party to the agreement was quite willing that the document be made public, the Government insisted on secrecy. It would not even let Members of this House have access to a copy of the
June 26, 1984

agreement. I find that deplorable. It is not the way for a government to act.
When people found out what was in the proposed final agreement, they complained, as they knew they had to, in order to get things changed. Senator Austin went up to the delta and made promises to all the people in that area that they would be able to present their case in some kind of public debate on the issue. But the proceedings from there on in remained secret, and Senator Austin's promise was proven to be just another Liberal promise: worthless.
There is with this agreement one unresolved and very important problem. It does not involve that many people but it rests on a principle. The prior rights of all the people of that area have not really been recognized and dealt with properly. One particular case is that of Canadian Reindeer and one Mr. William Nasogaluak. The reindeer herd, which had been owned and controlled by the Government of Canada for many years, was sold quite a few years ago to Mr. Nasogaluak. He was and is a very enterprising gentleman. He made a viable commercial success of reindeer herding in northern Canada, something that had never been done before. The idea had been started by the Government but it had never been commercially successful until it got into private hands. When that reindeer herd was sold to Mr. Nasogaluak it was quite evident that the Government had transferred to him the right to graze those reindeer within the reindeer grazing preserve established by Order in Council. Quite a proportion of that land had been transferred to COPE without consultation with Canadian Reindeer or Mr. Nasogaluak.
I consider this to be shabby treatment of a Canadian citizen by a shabby government. It is incumbent upon the Government of Canada to work out a deal with Canadian Reindeer, not tell them to work out some deal with COPE. They made their original deal with the Government of Canada. If the Government refuses to do this, it would be my suggestion that Mr. Nasogaluak has an extremely good case in law because I think the Government has broken its contract with him. Certainly he has an extremely good moral case.
The Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has gone out of his way in this agreement to protect the prior interests of oil and mining companies, as well as the Government itself; but when it comes to an Inuvialuit, he finds himself completely out of the picture. This has to be resolved.
To go back to the agreement proper, it has some good points. It is not my job as a Member of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition to overly dwell on the good points; they have all been presented to this House by the Parliamentary Secretary, the Hon. Member for Abitibi (Mr. Gingras), so I will concentrate on some of the points that are not quite as good.
I think those bad points were summarized for me by an old pensioner, an Inuvialuit himself, whom I visited in the old folks' home in Inuvik-shortly after the signing of the agreement in Tuktoyaktuk. He said that the only thing the agreement means for hims is that once a year he will receive in the mail a little piece of paper that is going to tell him how wealthy he is. That is all he is going to get out of it. He is not going to get a piece of land, a house or any money for the few
Western Arctic Agreement
remaining years he has to live. All he can see himself getting out of it is this piece of paper telling him he has lots of money. But where is it? There are no dollar bills for his pocket. He does not get a cheque; he gets nothing.
That is the other side of the story. In my opinion, this results from the rather socialistic and collectivist nature of the agreement. I can see why we have that type of agreement dealing with collectivities rather than individuals. First of all, that is the policy of the present Government of Canada and especially that of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who ran as a left-wing candidate in the recent Liberal leadership convention. Negotiatiors and advisers to native organizations are frequently of this bent. It is unfortunate, but I guess of necessity native organizations very often become mirror images of the bureaucracies with which they have to deal.
In the Inuvialuit community, many individuals have excelled in many fields, such as industry, trade and commerce, in the arts and many others. I venture to suggest that there are more millionnaires per thousand of population among the Inuvialuit component of our population than any other. But in the negotiating process over many years these people were generally concerned with their own affairs. They did not really get involved in the long, slow process. As a result, the individual point of view was lost because people who are individualistical-ly inclined were going about their own business. It is only when the final agreement was initialled that an action group was put together.
I would like to present some of the views of that Inuvialuit action group to the House. We know that 80 per cent of the population found in favour of the agreement and voted in that way. However, there is still one-fifth of the population with a different point of view. That point of view deserves to be heard. There was concern about the institutional nature of the agreement. One has only to look at a list of the institutions which are to be set up pursuant to the agreement. There are six or seven community corporations, each with a game council. There is the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation, the Inuvialuit Land Corporation, the Inuvialuit Development Corporation, the Inuvialuit Investment Corporation, the Inuvialuit Environmental Impact Review Board, the Inuvialuit Environmental Impact Screening Committee, the Inuvialuit Research Advisory Council and the Inuvialuit Wildlife Management Advisory Council. There are two of those, one for the Territories and one for the Yukon. There is the Inuvialuit Comprehensive Settlement Arbitration Board and various panels made up under that Board. There is the Inuvialuit Approval Authority, the Inuvialuit Game Council, the Porcupine-Cariboo Management Board, the Fisheries Joint Management Committee, the Yukon North Slope Annual Conference, the Inuvialuit Social Development Fund and its trustees, the Inuvialuit trust, the Inuvialuit Land Administration and the Inuvialuit Land Use Planning. There are two sub-groups of that, one for the Territories and one for the Yukon.

June 26, 1984
Western Arctic Agreement
You can see from that, Mr. Speaker, that it is a very institutionalized approach to life. It was a concern that any profits derived from economic development ventures or disposition of land or anything else would be eaten up in administrative costs. The 20 per cent of the people who opposed the agreement argued in favour of a cash settlement with some cash coming into the hands of individuals. They wanted guaranteed hunting and trapping rights. Other Inuvialuit wanted individual title to land rather than collective title to land. I think it is incumbent that the other side of the argument be heard at this time as well as the majority view.
Under this agreement, the 2,500 beneficiaries will share in some 5,000 square miles of 71-A land-that is land with mineral rights-and some 30,000 square miles of so-called 71-B land to which the mineral rights are not attached. This land will be free from the power of expropriation by any government other than the federal Government. It will also be free from taxation. However, that does not mean to say that improvements made upon the land will be exempt from taxation.
Just to put it in perspective, the land part of the over-all settlement area, a lot of it being water, is about the same size as the Provinces of Newfoundland, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and you can throw in Prince Edward Island for good measure. That is the type of area we are talking about under this agreement. In addition to that there will be cash payments of over $152 million over the period of time up until 1997. There is also the economic enhancement fund of $10 million, which was the buy-out for the 10 per cent bid differential which the Parliamentary Secretary has already referred to, and a social development fund of some $7.5 million. That brings the cash payments up to a total of $169.5 million, if my arithmetic is correct.
In addition to that, through one of their institutions the Inuvialuit have the right to borrow at an 8 per cent rate of interest to a maximum outstanding amount of $87.5 million. In financial terms you can see that the settlement is reasonably generous.
There are some additional concerns with this Bill which I have raised previously so I do not want to go into a great deal of detail about them. However, I would like to have them on the record. First, there is a very unusual nature of the tenure to some of this land. I foresee difficulties in the future. If you cannot sell something, do you really own it? That is a question which has always bothered me. There are constraints put on the disposition of some of this land. I do not know what could happen if you wanted to mortgage some of it to get funds with which to develop the land. I do not know whether that is possible. Just the other day we dealt with that problem with respect to the Cree-Naskapi Act and the necessity of writing provisions into the Act so that mortgages could be held on the land. I do not know if we are going to run into similar difficulties here.
There is a very complex regulatory process set up pursuant to this agreement. There are a number of advisory boards in addition to the regulatory system which presently exists. It is
going to slow things down and make it very difficult and expensive to go through this process. I suspect that at some point in the future people will look back and realize that they have tied themselves up so badly that they cannot then do the things they want to. That possibility also arises.
Another criticism which I have of the Bill is that there is nothing in it immediately for the elderly people. The old people had tough times in the past because it was pretty hard to make a living 50, 60 or 100 years ago in the Arctic areas before we had proper transportation and the other things we have today. Some of the old people went through some rough times and I do not see them getting anything out of this agreement. In my opinion, the old people should benefit more than anyone else. They should at least receive a half decent pension. The younger folks have education and the opportunities which we have in Canada today. I would prefer that the old people get something out of this rather than being neglected. That is what it looks like is happening to me.
Let us take another brief look at the proposed corporate structure. It is important to do this. Several things happened with the Alaskan settlement which was made some time ago. The old couple who were living in an old shack somewhere out in the bush before the settlement are still there with a fish net. Their lot does not seem to have improved very much. The settlement in Alaska created a new class of elite. The people who are involved in the corporate structure sit in their cork-lined boardrooms, draw big salaries, deal with millions of dollars and have a great old time. Somehow that has not filtered down to the little people.
Many objections have been brought up in Alaska. Tom Berger has been appointed to look at the agreement. That is something we want to avoid in Canada. If we make an agreement we do not want to have to say 15 years later it was a mistake. It is pretty important to study this. If you take the agreement and try to put all these institutions and bodies corporate in order, it comes out in kind of a spider's web pattern. The Inuvialuit Regional Corporation is stuck in the middle. One way or another it controls all the other organizations. It controls the Inuvialuit Development Corporation and the Inuvialuit Investment Corporation. Those two are set up to receive the cash payments. The Inuvialuit Land Corporation controls that too in a roundabout way as well as a direct way. The Inuvialuit Land Administration, which reports directly to the regional corporation, administers the land which is held by the Inuvialuit Land Corporation. Presumably it appoints directly the administrators and the ILC does not get to appoint the administrator.
Although in theory the community corporations are supposed to have some control over the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation, in reality I expect that it will work out the other way around. Even that is contemplated in the agreement. For instance, 71A/1 lands are supposed to be under the control of the various Inuvialuit community corporations, but the disposition or the control is always subject to the Inuvialuit Regional
June 26, 1984

Corporation. The trust, which is the repository of the funds that may be made available to individuals, is also subject to a substantial amount of control by the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation.
We can see that whoever controls and exercises this power within the Inuvialuit Regional Corporation will exercise power and control moneys of a magnitude undreamt of by anybody like myself. It will be a fantastic amount of control and power available to whoever manages to usurp that organization.
If that control is misused, then we can expect discontent. There is always a problem when a collective approach is taken, as we see in this agreement and in the Bill, instead of an individual approach to matters. Of course, there is some potential for abuse in every way it is done but I believe that by using the collective model or socialist model, that potential for abuse is exacerbated. All one needs to do is to see the various states in the world today. We find that those that have adopted that model can be far more abusive of the citizens of those countries than those that take an individualistic approach.
That is the gist of my presentation this afternoon. In conclusion, I repeat that the agreement is finished. What we have to do now is to try to make it work. That will be pretty tough. I suspect that making it work will be just as difficult a task as negotiating the agreement in the first place, if not more difficult. I simply want to add my rejoinder again, that I hope that the little people will not get shafted as has happened before. I fervently hope that we do not find ourselves, five decades down the road, standing up again in the House and saying that this did not work, let us try to renegotiate it again. I sincerely hope that this agreement works out to the benefit of all the people who live in the settlement area.

subtopic: WESTERN ARCTIC (INUVIALUIT) CLAIMS SETTLEMENT ACT MEASURE TO ESTABLISH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-49 which gives effect to the agreement that was reached between the Government of Canada and the Inuvialuit of the Northwest Territories, reaching into the Yukon.

June 26, 1984
Western Arctic Agreement
First, I would like to extend my congratulations to the Inuvialuit and the Minister. Our Party supports speedy passage of this legislation and the implementation of the agreement. While we support the speedy passage of this legislation, we want to note the very slow and painful process that has generally marked land claims and aboriginal claims negotiations and settlements in Canada over the past few years. That is especially true with regard to comprehensive claims.
It has been noted that this is only the second comprehensive claim to be settled, the first being the James Bay Agreement. I think every Member of the Flouse is aware of the frustration and problems that were involved in terms of implementation of that agreement, problems regarding the flow of funds, with regard to relations between the Government of Canada, the Government of Quebec and the new establishment of government by the James Bay Cree and Inuit.
I have particular concern in this Bill over Clause 3 which is really at the heart of the principle of the settlement of claims in the present government policy. Clause 3 states:
All native claims, rights, title and interests, whatever they may be, in and to the Territory, of all Inuvialuit, whatever they may be, are hereby extinguished-
Our Party has a great deal of concern over the idea that aboriginal claims must be extinguished before any settlement can be reached on those claims. Aboriginal people have been moving toward the concept that an aboriginal right per se is something that cannot be extinguished. Rather, it is something that should be recognized. Having recognized it, the Government of Canada or the province or territory should negotiate for use with that aboriginal people. We should be involved in a process of recognition of rights rather than seek to terminate those rights. The termination of rights smacks too much of a real estate process. Real estate processes do violence to the concept of land that the aboriginal peoples of Canada have. Their relationship to the land is more basic and cultural and spiritual, in such a way that a real estate process often does violence to it. For that reason we support them in their concern to find some other approach rather than out and out extinguishment.
I note that the Minister has said he would explore alternatives to extinguishment. I hope that an alternative can be found and that that alternative can be applied to the Inuvialuit as well as to other aboriginal peoples. We were very concerned about the slow progress in the settlement of comprehensive claims in British Columbia, for example, when the Haida, Heltsuk and Nuu Chah Nulth submitted claims both to their land and to some offshore resources. It took months and it stretched into years before the Government even accepted these claims for negotiation. This slowness in processing is very discouraging for aboriginal peoples. It is one of the reasons this is only the second agreement to be reached. I suppose it returns to the fact that the Department, through the Office of Native Claims, is really the judge, jury and executioner in terms of the entire aboriginal claims process.
Aboriginal people coming up against the Department find that it is very easy for them to be stonewalled. When they are stonewalled, they have no real process of appeal. We would like to see the entire claims process opened up and made more fair, in a way that aboriginal peoples would know that they had certain rights and processes to follow by law instead of being at the good favour of the Government.
When claims are recognized and accepted for negotiation, the Government is very slow in its different processes. For example, we are concerned about the Kaska Dene in northern British Columbia. They received only a quarter of the funding which they recognized as being necessary if they were to do an adequate job of researching their aboriginal claim. Having received only a quarter of their funds, their entire claim process is now in some difficulty. We must recognize that it is a very expensive process to establish what is a claim, to establish traditional patterns of land use and occupancy, and to establish traditional hunting, fishing and food-gathering processes. The research involved is very expensive. Having established a pattern of research, it is important that there be continuity, that it not be interrupted. As the Kaska Dene received only a quarter of their funding, and unless further funds flow fairly quickly, they will have some difficulty maintaining continuity. There is a possibility of fairly rapid development of the mineral, timber and hydroelectric resources in their area. It is important that they be able to conduct the research now rather than have to wait. Also they are in a situation where some of their traditional lands overlap some of those under claim by the Council of Yukon Indians. It is important that they have funding now so that they can conduct the necessary research to solve any overlap situations on a fair and equitable basis between themselves and their good friends in the Council of Yukon Indians.
The Special Committee on Indian Self-Government recommended that there be a new claims process. This is something that we in our Party would heartily endorse. It recommended a claims process wherein the Department was not the judge, jury and executioner, a claims process which recognized the legitimate claims of Indian peoples and other aboriginal peoples in settled areas. Presently there is a concept, which the Government follows, whereby it says that aboriginal claims in settled areas such as in southwestern British Columbia have been superseded by law. In effect, what we are saying by that process is that aboriginal rights, claims and title have been superseded by might. Might makes right is what the concept superseded by law means. We should open up the process to recognize that if people had basic aboriginal rights 200 years or 300 years ago and if they never negotiated those rights away, they are still intact. The concept that they can be superseded by law really says that they have been taken away by force. That is not a concept of justice to which most Canadians would want to subscribe.
Another area which we would like to see changed in a future land claims policy would be the removal of the present separation between settlement of land claims and settlement of
June 26, 1984

political issues. For aboriginal people, political rights are an integral part of the claims which they are seeking to put forward. Also the Special Committee on Indian Self-Government, through a long series of hearings, established very clearly that aboriginal peoples had political rights and exercised those political rights long before the coming of European colonists to this continent. Those political rights are the essence of their aboriginal rights. To talk about an aboriginal land claims process which neglects those political rights does violence to their whole concept of the land.
The Union of British Columbia Indian Chiefs has a slogan: "The land is the culture". Basically, land, culture, spiritual values and political rights are interrelated among aboriginal peoples. To say that we are willing to negotiate land rights here but that we are not willing to discuss political rights which have to be resolved in a separate forum, is to do violence to the basic understanding of aboriginal peoples of themselves and of their relationship to the land.
We support the whole concept that political rights should be involved in the settlement of aboriginal claims. Coming from British Columbia, I am concerned that while the federal Government moves very slowly in the settlement of claims, the Government of British Columbia is actively stonewalling and preventing the claims.
For a number of years now significant progress on a number of claims had not been possible until the Province of British Columbia moved on the claim of the Nishga people. The process has been very slow and very painful. Anything the federal Government or the Canadian public could do to move the reactionary, right-wing Government of British Columbia toward a more positive recognition of aboriginal claims would be helpful. It would help to solve a long-standing injustice. It would help Indian people of British Columbia to take their rightful place in the culture and economy of British Columbia.
We want to see the claims process speeded up. It should recognize the rights of aboriginal peoples in Canada. Whether it be the Indians, the Metis or the Inuit, they should have their rights recognized. They should have a decent land base from which they can operate economically so that they will no longer be at the bottom statum of society in terms of the economy. There is no reason that being a member of the aboriginal peoples should be equated with poverty. However, that is the situation in Canada, because in effect these people have been robbed of their rights.
It is important to institute a new and more speedy land claims policy which will not extinguish those rights but will recognize them. This policy should not try to separate those rights from their political rights. It should see them as being integral and it should recognize their rights to a decent economic base.
With those few remarks, I am pleased that the Inuvialuit have made some progress in the negotiation of their claim with the federal Government. They negotiated, as most aboriginal people have had to do, under considerable pressure. I congratulate them on their settlement. Like all Members, we hope
Western Arctic Agreement
that it works for their betterment. We look forward to speedy passage of this Bill.

speakeroldname: Mr. Stan J. Hovdebo (Prince Albert) moved:
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CHANGING NAME AND EXPANDING RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of (a) changing the Canadian Wheat Board's name to the Canadian Grains Board (b) expanding the Board's responsibility by placing the major grains-barley, corn, flax, oats, rapeseed, rye, soybeans and wheat-under its jurisdiction and by giving the Board full responsibility for marketing all feed grains delivered to primary elevators in Canada.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased that the other matter was cleared up in so short a time.
The agricultural industry across Canada is in trouble. In the last three or four months, there has been an increase of almost 150 per cent in the number of farm bankruptcies. At the rate we are going, there will be fewer and fewer farms across the country every year to the point where the agricultural industry is bound to suffer. It is too bad that an industry the workforce of which at one time made up approximately 90 per cent of the population of Canada is now down to a workforce of 5 per cent of the population and dwindling fast.
The situation is particularly bad because the industry could support many, many more farmers than it is now supporting. The consolidation that is going on may be good for the individual farmer but is not good for the country as a whole. Therefore, although this particular motion deals with one small part of the problem, I feel that it is important to put this
motion before the House and have it discussed as part of the solution to the problem.
This particular motion deals with only one part of the agricultural industry, that part of the agricultural industry which is the growing of grain on the Prairies. That grain is the key to a great portion of the money from foreign exchange which Canada earns every year. Therefore, it is very important that we have a stable structure which will allow grain to be gathered, shipped and sold. That is the duty of the Canadian Wheat Board.
The mandate of the Canadian Wheat Board is to buy the grain, sell it at the best possible price and turn over as much of that sale money to the farmer as is possible. That is the key to the Wheat Board. It operates in the best interests of the farmer, not in the best interests of a variety of other people who handle the grain between the farmer and the consumer.
The global problem is that we do not have a system in place which allows income security for farmers. To some extent, I suppose I am being remiss in my duty in treating only a small portion of the problem rather than the total problem. A couple of weeks ago my colleague, the Hon. Member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), brought forward Bill C-232 which dealt with parity of prices for farm products. That Bill was sent to committee to be discussed. The very fact that that Bill was sent to committee indicates that the House recognizes that agriculture generally is in trouble and that we must take a good global look at what should be done.
If the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) were here today, he would stand and say that agriculture in Canada is doing better than agriculture in any other country in the world. Then he would list all sorts of good things which he is doing for agriculture or which the Government claims it is doing for agriculture. Let us look at a few of the things which the Government says it is doing.
It claims that the farmers are being well financed and are better off because the Farm Credit Corporation is in place. It can be interpreted that way, but it can also be interpreted that the interest rates of the Farm Credit Corporation are probably the biggest factor in the number of farm bankruptcies.
In the last year the Government has dealt with freight rates. That is a very important factor in the bringing of grain to market. How did the Government deal with it? It increased those rates. If we take a look at that process to find out what the rates will be in the next few years, we will see that the increase has only started and that there will be many more increases. Every one of those increases puts farmers in the position in which there will be a much smaller chance of
June 26, 1984

making a living. Many more farmers will leave their farms because they will not be able to make an adequate living.
Both opposition Parties have often asked the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of Agriculture if they would relieve some of the pressure on farmers by taking the tax off fuel. They tell us that it sounds like a good idea, but they will not do it. The Government has made no effort to improve the situation as far as farmers are concerned.
That seems like a rather convoluted approach to a motion which deals directly and specifically with the Canadian Wheat Board, but I am trying to put forth the idea that what we need in all approaches to agriculture-if we are to deal with tax on fuels, freight rates and interest rates-is an income security structure which will allow farmers to know that they will get the best possible return for their labour. We are talking about a structure which the farmer can recognize as fair. That was the basis of the development of the Wheat Board initially and it is still the basis of its operation. It seems incongruous that what works well for wheat should not be extended to other crops.
For example, at this moment we probably have the best example in years of what can happen to grain if there is not a structure which protects the farmer. Last fall when farmers began selling rapeseed and canola, they received approximately $5 per bushel. Since that time, the price has increased to as much as $16 per bushel. Most of that grain was sold by farmers at $5, $6, $7 or $8 per bushel. That grain was stored. Recently it was released into the market at $16 per bushel. Who received the profit? Not the farmers who planted the grain, took the risk, hauled it into town and sold it to pay for their production. The people who received the advantage of the increase were those people who speculated on the price of grain. They bought the rapeseed and held it. They did nothing. They did not work. It was no effort for them. Sometimes they did not even hold the grain. They simply held a piece of paper for a six-month period and then sold the grain at $16 per bushel. They received a profit of approximately $10 per bushel. Had that money been turned into the system, as it would have been had the grain been sold under the Wheat Board, it would have been spread out among the farmers who produced rapeseed last year.
I grew up on a farm before the Wheat Board was established and I can remember very vividly my father selling wheat at 75 cents per bushel in the fall. At that time he hoped that he could hold on to at least half of his grain in order that he could sell it for $1.75 in the spring. In the spring, the Winnipeg Grain Exchange would have manipulated the market to the point where the grain which they had held and had bought from the farmers for 75 cents per bushel in the fall would have increased in order that the Grain Exchange could make $1 per bushel. Again, that profit was made with no effort and no risk. The grain was bought and they sold it when they had manipulated the price of grain upward. That was the reason the Wheat Board was established, by the Conservatives. The same thing is going on right now.
Canadian Wheat Board
My motion suggests that the Government take a look at extending the structure, which now controls wheat, barley and oats sold for the export market, to cover other grains in order that other farmers are not ripped off in the same manner as they have been in the past; as they were with the change in canola grain costs from $5 to $16 per bushel. Possibly the return would have been less than $16 per bushel, but if some farmers could afford to keep enough to receive $16 per bushel, they would be the only ones in that whole block who probably did well.
What I am really doing in this motion, Mr. Speaker, is plunking for fairness and against speculation. Farmers who did not grow up in the days when speculation ran rampant, do not realize how well they are served by the Wheat Board. Many of the younger farmers feel that they could go out on the market themselves and do better. I would challenge any of them to do so. A number of years ago we had a rather long discussion on the possibilities of putting all of the feed grains on the open market. The result of those discussions was very interesting. Although a portion of the feed grain is sold on the open market, Mr. Speaker, there still is a certain amount of it sold through the Wheat Board. It is not surprising that when the Wheat Board does well, when it sells well on the export market, the open market then does well, because what is happening is that the Wheat Board is taking off the domestic market a certain amount of feed, which allows the prices to go up. That would not happen if that dual system was not in place. Prices for the cattlemen in years when the Wheat Board sells a lot of grain overseas would not go up the way they do. And in those years when the Wheat Board does not sell well overseas, the price of grain goes down, which is good for the cattlemen but not for the producer of feed. That kind of up and down roller-coaster approach to agriculture is what we had back in the 1930s, but it is not what we want now. It is still happening with canola. It would be a good approach to put before the grain growers of Canada at least an opportunity to take a look at how that kind of market would work.
The Winnipeg Grain Exchange is a well established group of people. It claims it is helping the farmers. It buys as low as possible and sells as high as possible. In the process it makes money. It gets that money from either the consumer, because he pays more for his grain, or from the producer, because he receives less for his grain. No one can argue with that. The grain exchange will tell you that sometimes it loses but, obviously, on the average it does not, because if it lost or even if it just balanced out, the grain exchange would soon disappear. Therefore, it is there to make as much profit as possible, and that profit must come either from the producer or from the consumer. The grain exchange will tell you how good it is for the market, but it has never proven that it is anything other than a parasite on that market because it takes money out of the pockets of the farmers and the consumers.
The Canadian Wheat Board, Hon. Members will say, is a good operation. It buys its grain from the farmers and sells it on the world market. It returns as much of that profit as

June 26, 1984
Canadian Wheat Board
possible to the farmer. Why is it then not possible to take every grain which is produced and put it through the same kind of structure so that the farmers receive the maximum return from their efforts and labour? This habit of living off the farmers should not go on. What is happening, as I said at the beginning of my remarks, is that we have a situation which becomes less fair as time goes on, to the point where fewer and fewer farmers are going to survive. It is very disappointing to realize there are places where a few years ago ten farmers lived quite well on what now only support two farmers. The surprising part of it is that statistics show that the amount of income tax paid by the farmer who is now ten times as big as he was before, is actually less than paid by the farmer next door to him with the half section or the section. We are developing an agricultural system in the grain country which is not providing for as many people as it possibly could, and that is not good for the country.
Let us take a look at the organizations and the global structure of agriculture and try to develop some sensible and logical ways of making sure that the farmer will get enough to survive on. One of the ways we might help is to take a look at the Wheat Board and at least develop a stable structure for our marketing.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CHANGING NAME AND EXPANDING RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to speak on the motion which has been put before the House by the Hon. Member. I wondered, listening to the Hon. Member speak, how many farmers who operate in the free market system would still be alive if it is true that they are all broke. However, that is not the case. The Hon. Member has put forward a reasonable argument for his motion and I understand that the strong argument for the motion is the concept upon which the Wheat Board has operated since its beginning, that is the concept of pooling, of sharing, so that the price at the beginning of the year for the farmer is the same as at the end of the year. That process-of which we are very proud-was put in place by a Conservative Government to meet a problem which was in place some 50 years ago. Of course, many things have changed since that time, but something which has not changed is that the Canadian Wheat Board has served the western farmers well.
I want to put forward a couple of suggestions to the Hon. Member. First, we object to his suggestion that the name of the Canadian Wheat Board be changed. Every farmer, whether old or young, recognizes the good service of the Canadian Wheat Board in this country. The Canadian Wheat Board has an international reputation of being able to sell the farmers' grain at a reasonable and often better price than other countries have been able to get on the international market. I know that the Hon. Member is somewhat jealous that the Progressive Conservative Party brought in the Canadian Wheat Board. Of course, every time he gets on a political platform in Saskatchewan, I know he has trouble swallowing the fact that a Progressive Conservative Government brought this Canadian Wheat Board into being. That is probably why he wants to change the name. He is not satisfied to just bring other grains into the market and leave the name the same. He would rather
change the name and hope that the New Democratic Party could then take some credit for it. We take exception to that for two reasons: first, it was brought in by an excellent government some sixty years ago, and, second, the international reputation of the Canadian Wheat Board is well known; there is no need to change the name and try to get other countries in this world to understand that we now have a new operation in Canada which is attempting to sell wheat, oats and barley in that market.
That is one part of the motion with which I have difficulty. The second part is this. The Hon. Member was not clear, and I would like to have asked him this question. If the NDP were in power would they impose this on Canadian farmers? We all know their record of defending western farmers when it came to a change in the Constitution. Their leader was all too willing to side with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and impose a Constitution. When it came to the National Energy Program, the NDP could not run up behind the Government quickly enough to impose that on western Canada. Therefore I ask if they would impose this on the farmers of western Canada if they were in power.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this Party would not do that. We want to try to get farmers to work together rather than against one another on how to market their grains. This was the difficulty we faced during the Crow debate. The solution to the problem is that if the farmers of western Canada make the decision that they want to market canola, rapeseed or flaxseed through the Canadian Wheat Board, then we ought to respect that decision. But that is not the message the Members of my Party have gotten from their constituents. The question is still open. In fact, when the wheat pools did a survey in 1981 they found the majority of farmers were opposed to this move.
Today many farmers have the opportunity to judge the performance of the Canadian Wheat Board. The most important crop in this respect is canola. It is a cash crop to many farmers. They are not interested in getting an initial price; they want the cash up front. Canola is not the sole crop for most farmers. It is grown as a cash crop because in the West, particularly on the Prairies, a farmer does not have the opportunity to grow a variety of crops. He is limited to a certain number, and that is one of the reasons that most of the canola growers in western Canada are satisfied with the present system.
The assumption that if you grow canola and sell it at the beginning of the year the price will be less than at the end of the year is just that, an assumption. In some years that is the case, in some years it is not. The assumption that the grain companies are always the winners, along with the speculators on the Winnipeg Grain Exchange, if you want to call them that, is not true. They establish a market, a price, which in turn establishes freedom. The strongest argument by farmers opposed to putting these grains under the Canadian Wheat Board is that they want some element of freedom.
June 26, 1984

Then we have the argument of the feed grain users, the cattlemen, hog and poultry growers. They also question the value of having feed grain under the Canadian Wheat Board. This was the case up until 1974, when the decision was made to allow feed grains some freedom. The question is still open as to whether that is the way it should stay, or if it should revert to the Canadian Wheat Board. The 1981 survey showed that 55 per cent of the farmers in western Canada wished the system to remain the same as it was in 1974. I have to say again that I respect that decision.
There is a point I think the Wheat Board ought to take very seriously. If they want the feed grains under their jurisdiction they ought to show some flexibility. Many farmers along the southern part of the Prairies have been able to find markets in the U.S. for their feed grains at substantially higher prices than they could in their own locales. Yet the Wheat Board turns down every one of those export permits. That is totally unfair and it does not show the kind of flexibility which is needed in the interests of western farmers, should the Hon. Member's motion turn into reality and all feed grains go under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. Farmers say it is nice to have the advantage of pooling and sharing, it is nice to have these experts out in the world selling their grain, but then they are faced with this situation and they wonder about the flexibility of the Wheat Board.
I think it is clear that while the Member's motion has something to offer, it is an open question which farmers ought to be discussing. They ought to be giving their elected representatives their views on whether the system should change, but there is no way it ought to be imposed upon them.
There are arguments on both sides of the coin, both of which are very important, such as imposing a name change on the Canadian Wheat Board. Cash cropping is important to many western farmers, but they will not be able to do that under the Canadian Wheat Board. Western farmers are concerned that the initial prices set for grains are far too low given the international market. They question the kind of service they would have if everything was under the jurisdiction of the Wheat Board. These things have to be addressed, so rather than move too quickly on this motion, there are many other things we should look at. I have in mind things like the Bracken formula, things like producer cars, revisions to the Crow rate, updating of the elevator system, branchlines, West Coast and East Coast efficiency in moving grain, and the opportunity to have value added industries on the Prairies such as meat, grain and canola processing. These are all very essential things which we must move on very quickly, perhaps even more quickly than on the suggestion the Hon. Member is making.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Eva Cote (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CHANGING NAME AND EXPANDING RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before the House today proposes that the government should consider the advisability of changing the Canadian Wheat Board's name to the Canadian Grains Board and expanding the Board's responsibility by
Canadian Wheat Board
placing the major grains-barley, corn, flax, oats, rapeseed, rye, soybeans and wheat-under its jurisdiction and by giving the Board full responsibility for marketing all feed grains delivered to primary elevators in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, this motion may have substantial repercussions on the Canadian grain and oil seed industry and on the producers, organizations, government and non-government boards and private companies that constitute the industry. At the present time, the Canadian Wheat Board, and I may add, Mr. Speaker, that in 1985 the Board will be celebrating its fiftieth birthday and I think it would be appropriate to wish the Board, somewhat in advance, a very happy birthday and offer it our best wishes for a successful future.
The Board is the only marketing body for wheat, oats and barley grown in the Prairies and destined for export or for human consumption in Canada. The Board may also sell feed barley, oats and wheat on the domestic feed grain market. The Canadian Wheat Board's primary purpose is to sell as much grain as it can at the best possible price and to maximize returns for Prairie wheat, oats and barley producers.
Although the Canadian Wheat Board plays a major role in the Canadian grain industry, we must not forget that the industry includes a wide range of government and non-government bodies that work together to transport grain to Canadian exporters and consumers. I shall, if I may, take a few moments to talk about the principal members of the Canadian grain industry. I shall, of course, leave enough time for the Hon. Member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave) to make a few comments before six o'clock, because I would be very interested to hear what he has to say.
Producers are the most important group in the industry. Without them, the Canadian grain industry would not exist. Grain is produced in all Canadian provinces. According to the 1981 Census, and this is very important, Mr. Speaker, Canada had 162.8 million acres of farm land in 1981 with 76.5 million acres being farmed and 24 million acres in fallow, most of the land being used for growing grain and oil seeds. Still in 1981, 127,359 farming operations stated they grew wheat, 81,417 oats, 102,190 barley, 33,543 corn, 12,819 rye, 12,083 flax, 10,655 soya beans and 14,804 canola. This shows how diversified grain production is in this country. Farmers in all provinces stated they grew at least one of these grains or oil seeds. The four provinces where most of these farmers are concentrated are, of course, the Prairie provinces: Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta, and Ontario. Quebec, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Prince Edward Island also have a substantial number of grain operations.
According to estimates, total profits from grain and oil seed amounted to $7 billion in 1983. Grain producers are therefore a major force in determining the structure, components and functioning of the grain industry. Although the Canadian

June 26, 1984
Canadian Wheat Board
Wheat Board is a federal body and is subject to federal laws, it is above all an organization that is concerned with selling wheat, oats and barley on behalf of Canadian producers. Over the years, producers have established the marketing system they want to facilitate grain sales. In his motion, the Hon. Member is suggesting that the Government consider the advisability of changing the name of the Board. Mr. Speaker, I think most Hon. Members would agree that it would be very high-handed of the Government to want to set unilaterally the conditions for the sale of a specific grain or oil seed.
We recall that in the seventies, producers decided, by referendum, to maintain a free market for canola. Today, canola is sold on the free market. Rye and flax grown in the Prairies are also sold on the free market. Grain corn produced in Ontario, Quebec and Manitoba is also sold on the free market. Oleaginous grains marketing boards do not sell all the harvests of producers, as do the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board. This board is responsible for buying and selling the wheat grown in Ontario, except for wheat sold among producers for agricultural purposes. The Ontario board must seek the best market price for any Ontario-grown wheat, in accordance with well-established marketing principles. There is another kind of board, such as the Ontario Soybean Producers Marketing Board which negotiates for producers rather than representing them.
Just to say a few words about the Ontario Soybean Producers Marketing Board, it was established in 1949 to improve marketing conditions for Ontario-grown soybeans. Every year it negotiates the conditions of soybean sales to dealers. However, the producer sells his harvest directly to a processor, a cattleman or a grain agency. Cooperatives and companies which buy and sell grains in their own name also provide worthwhile services for the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board. Cooperatives and private companies own and operate primary and terminal elevators as well as sales outlets for farm and processing equipment.
Mr. Speaker, I think 1 do not have enough time to explain to the House the ideal way in which the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board operate. Keeping in mind the outstanding business done by grain producers and the quality of services offered over the years by the Canadian Wheat Board to all the producers who joined together within organizations or institutions to market their products, it does not seem advisable, as suggested by the Hon. Member of the Official Opposition who spoke before me, to change anything in the structure of the Canadian Wheat Board.
In Canada, there are also grain companies, the first and foremost being farmer co-ops. There is no need to insist on the value of the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the Alberta Wheat Pool, the Manitoba Pool Elevators, the United Grain Producers in the Prairies, United Co-ops in Ontario and the
Cooperative federee in Quebec. It is my view that all those groups, working for the welfare of grain producers, have demonstrated their worth.
Mr. Speaker, I would like to leave some time to the Honourable member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Hargrave), who wishes to speak on the matter, but I want to state that the motion put by the Honourable member for the new Democratic Party is rather well stated, although I wonder if all the possible ramifications have been examined. Although farmers are not unanimous, and indeed other interested groups, and this has been a fact for a long time, the same motion has been put forward on various occasions by the New Democratic Party. In fact, the same member introduced a motion that was almost identical in 1980. It has been said that his motivation was sincere, which I do not doubt. But since he keeps reviving the idea, it seems to me that his party is not aware of all the evidence pointing to the practical problems that the implementation of that concept will raise. Books and treatises have been written on the pros and cons of a marketing board and other systems. And although the Canadian and provincial governments are giving much attention to the issue, the choice finally should rest with producers. They are most directly involved. As has already been mentioned in the debate, there is no evidence that the establishment of a national Board would get significant support accross the nation, and even among the main crop growers. Clearly producers still want some flexibility in their operations.
However, Mr. Speaker, it is clear to us that after 49 years of existence, the Canadian Wheat Board has been fulfilling its mandate. I was happy to hear the honourable member from the Official Opposition, who spoke before me, state the Canadian Wheat Board was an internationally famous agency that was a credit to Canada and Canadian grain growers.

subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CHANGING NAME AND EXPANDING RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) has put forward a Private Members' Motion in two parts. The first part is to change the name of the Canadian Wheat Board. Let me quickly and simply say that I cannot support that, primarily because of the implications that flow from the second part of his motion. That is what I propose to comment on briefly.
The second part of the motion proposes to expand the board's responsibilities by placing the major grains; barley, corn, flax, oats, rapeseed, rye, soybeans and wheat under its jurisdiction and by giving the board full responsibility for marketing all feed grains delivered to primary elevators in Canada. Of course, by implication, that is primarily in western Canada.
Let me say that I cannot support this proposal that would put our domestic feed grains delivered to our western country elevators completely under the authority of the Wheat Board as the Wheat Board's total responsibility.
June 26, 1984

This proposal quite properly invites comment on our so-called domestic feed grain policy. This most important issue, especially for western Canada, was deliberately and skilfully avoided during the six-month Crow debate last year. It is an issue that should the debated publicly and here in Parliament, along with the so-called Canadian Livestock Feed Board, when an appropriate occasion should develop.
All domestic feed grains may now be delivered to our western country elevators by producers with the appropriate permit book. But for livestock feeders to get that feed grain out of the elevators for local livestock feeding is quite another matter.
Of course, the Board's policy is to eventually ship all or nearly all of the feed grains for export. It can be purchased from the country elevators after the necessary permit is obtained from the Wheat Board, but at substantially higher prices than is available for deliveries of that same feed grain, even after allowing for a modest elevator charge.
It must surely be obvious that our domestic feed grain policy must be thoroughly reviewed and changed significantly to serve its biggest total market for that feed grain. Surely that is our total livestock feeding industry, essentially cattle and hogs, especially in western Canada.
It should be obvious to all of us that the greatest potential value-added industry for our grain sector in western Canada is not our flour milling, our meat packing and processing industry or even the oil seed crushing industry. It is by far the total livestock feeding industry for cattle and hogs and utilizing huge amounts of western barley and oats right in western Canada. That is by far our most important value-added industry in agriculture in western Canada.
If we are going to change our feed grains policy in the West, let us allow our country elevators to serve this industry by taking it in for local storage and also selling it locally on an open market, right out of the same elevator.
The well known and outdated corn competitive pricing formula should be scrapped. If a new feed grain pricing formula is necessary it could be related to the barley export price worked back to the country elevators.
The proposal by the Hon. Member for Prince Albert would be the kiss of death for this tremendous potential for a total livestock feeding industry all across western Canada. Let us make some changes in our feed grain policy, but let us make those changes work for our western agricultural future, where the feed grains are produced and where the value-added industries are logical and can be done most efficiently.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subsubtopic: ADVISABILITY OF CHANGING NAME AND EXPANDING RESPONSIBILITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 127 seeks government consideration of the advisability of changing the Canadian Wheat Board's name to the Canadian Grains Board and expanding the Board's responsibility by placing the major grains under its jurisdiction and by giving the Board full responsibility for marketing all feed grains delivered to primary elevators in Canada.
Canadian Wheat Board
In essence, the motion seeks the universal adoption of the Board marketing system for the grains marketed commercially in Canada and consequently the elimination of the open market system which continues to be used for many of the major grains sold for domestic use in this country.
Public controversy over the relative merits and shortcomings of these two marketing systems has waxed and waned with strong feelings held on both sides, ever since the Board marketing system was first employed as a temporary measure to tide over a period of market uncertainty at the end of World War I. Thus, the debate on this motion is simply the revival and continuation of the debate on an issue which has not been resolved to the satisfaction of all producers over the past 60 years.
Let us review that debate. It should be recognized that the development of the Canadian Wheat Board marketing system was related closely to the importance of wheat exports to the economy of the West and the history of efforts in western Canada to develop a marketing agency to deal with its major customers abroad. It had little to do with the appropriate marketing systems for sales within Canada. In considering the motion which is simply a continuation of the historic debate, the debate over the best marketing system for grain is often influenced by the nature of grain or oil seed under discussion, the type of markets to which this is to be sold and whether domestic processing is an important part of that market. A further development of this debate relates to the discussion over domestic marketing of feed grains in Canada.
The decision by the Government to modify the marketing system for domestic feed grains in 1974 was mainly in response to problems perceived by users of food grains in Canada with respect to price equity and assurance of supply. At that time some producers again considered that the Government should place the marketing of all western feed grains under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board. Others considered that the open market system should be retained both for sales within the Prairie region and in the rest of Canada.
Some believed that the Canadian Wheat Board should be the only seller of feed grains to parts of the country outside the Prairies and that the Livestock Feed Board of Canada should be the sole buyer. However, the price would have to be negotiated between the two boards and no effective method for doing this could be found. Consequently, a new policy was developed to provide a national market for feed grains with prices established by the full interplay of supply and demand. This provided all users in Canada with access to feed grains in all regions of Canada.
The marketing system was changed to provide direct access to western supplies by users in all parts of Canada through the open market. Subsequently, arrangements were developed involving the Canadian Wheat Board and the Livestock Feed Board of Canada on a basis for sales of Canadian Wheat Board grains into the domestic feed market at corn competitive prices. This is a very condensed review of facts concerning
