associations and similar vehicles. The change in the Bank Act permitted the banks to become involved. Prior to that time, because there was not the variation in rates that there is today, the traditional understanding was that in order to cancel a mortgage there would be a three-month bonus to the mortgagor. During the recent period of dramatic increases and falls in interest rates, the three-month bonus was hidden in the body of the mortgage. It was used as another explanation for the penalty the person would have to pay to readjust a mortgage which would be based on the interest rate which was in effect at the time it was to be rearranged. Therefore, if a person took out a 20 per cent mortgage and the rate dropped to 12 per cent, that person would be required to pay 6 per cent on the commuted value of the mortgage over the life of the mortgage. That has created a misunderstanding. The public has been faced with the tremendous burden of serious penalties. Those penalties were imposed upon them and hidden in the body of the mortgage document. That has caused financial losses to a number of people.
I know of a number of people who wanted to move in order to upgrade their homes. When they attempted to sell their home, they found out that they had lost $3,000 to $6,000 in penalties on which they had not counted. Some of those people had received information which was incorrect, not from the lender but from the general public. At least this Bill spells out what they will encounter. However, I do not believe it is fair. It is legitimizing the clauses which were included in mortgage documents by the banks and the trust companies to protect themselves against great losses from a change in the interest rates. We must keep in mind that the banks have billions of dollars of non-interest bearing deposits. The banks can better afford losses than can the individual home owner.
We need to have mortgage interest stabilization. This subject has not been addressed nor has it been dealt with. However, we require stabilization to encourage home ownership which will bring it back up to the 70 per cent level. If that were done, it would create at least 100,000 additional housing starts per year, which would take close to one-quarter of a million people off the unemployment ranks. If we could get six of those, we could solve the major effect of unemployment in Canada. 1 do not believe it can be done by the Liberal Government. It has been unimaginative in its legislation. It has done nothing to help the people of Canada. Farmers have suffered and home owners have suffered.
On Friday, I spoke on Bill C-37. That legislation was intended to protect the mortgagee against an increased rate upon renewal. I gave statistics which indicated that the Bill would do very little for those individuals unless they had a five-year mortgage on a 10 per cent rate. If rates went up to 18 per cent they would get the difference between 12 per cent and 18 per cent, for a net of 6 per cent. In that case, the mortgage insurance plan would work, but it is being implemented at the wrong time.
During this period there have been some companies which have been extremely helpful. I would like to mention them because I have had hundreds of complaints from people who
could not afford the penalty which was imposed. I have had co-operation from a number of institutions. There are three institutions in particular with which I have had some success. One is National Trust. I went to the regional vice-president and he, in turn, sent me to the regional manager. I had success with the Canada Trust which, through its executive vice-president, gave me some consideration. I had great help in several cases from the Bank of Montreal. But the examples I give you were in the minority. There were many other financial institutions which just said, "Tough bananas. Tell your constituents to lump it". Those institutions were totally unfair and unrealistic with these people. However, I did want to mention the three institutions I had success with because they were a great help to my constituents. They were fair to them and have assisted them.
The Hon. Member from British Columbia-I cannot think of his riding-has brought out the fact that we have to provide somehow long-term mortgages with reasonable interest rates. There was a committee hearing today at which, unfortunately,
I was not present. The hearing related to agri-bonds to help lower interest rates for farmers. A possible expansion of that may be one route which could be taken. I have not investigated this route nor have I reviewed it, but possibly through that system we could experiment with providing long-term interest rates so that when a man bought a home he could buy a 20- year mortgage, as he was able to do in the past. In the United States until recently, that 20-year mortgage meant that the rate you established when you bought that home lasted for the full life of the mortgage, and at the end of 20 years your mortgage would be paid off unless you refinanced. We must provide some stabilization in the interest market along those lines in order to help people to own homes.
What this Bill provides is a rate differential between the mortgage and the prevailing rate. As you know, mortgage rates are traditionally at a higher rate due to the risk factor. And there is a risk in a mortgage as compared to a money instrument. But the interest rates are higher. Part of the mortgagor's risk was taken into consideration through this higher interest rate. I feel that we should maintain the three-month penalty. I understand that it cannot be done. I understand there must be some compromise between the three-month penalty and something to assist the large mortgagors, but possibly a formula cold be developed where all mortgages, no matter of what length, could have a three-month penalty. On top of that there could be an additional penalty of one-half month for each 1 per cent variation in interest rate, up to a maximum of a six-month penalty. The reason I suggest this is that it is a compromise to help the mortgagors and it will help the mortgagees. It is something which would work for both of them. The mortgagor would know that the maximum penalty he is going to suffer is six months. At least we have gone from the potential of three months at the low end to a six-month maximum penalty at the high end.
I believe this is a plan which should be investigated in committee. I will bring it forward myself in committee. I am
June 26, 1984

delighted to hear the Minister of State for Finance agree that there could be some compromise plan which would help all people.
We cannot afford this interest rate variation, the peaks and the lows. It can be stabilized if we get economic growth back in Canada, but I have seen no Bills go through this House which will encourage economic growth in the medium and small business sector. I must admit that our present upswing has been basically caused by the multinationals, particularly the automobile industry which is selling bigger cars. Chrysler came out with a new product which it is producing in Canada. That is the only thing which has brought us around. I noticed an article in the local Whitby Chamber of Commerce bulletin which says that bankruptcies were down this March from last March. My answer to it was to keep in mind that there have been so many bankruptcies over the last four years that there are fewer businesses to go bust. That is a critical problem with which we are dealing here in Canada. We need more entrepreneurs to create business and in turn to create jobs. Nothing has come down the pipes from this Government which is going to create jobs. It has made some minor adjustments in the Income Tax Act, of which I approve, but they are minor adjustments. They have made some minor adjustments in the research and development allowances for tax relief. But there is nothing to say to the Canadian people, "This is a great country. We will be behind you. We will simplify your life and make it easy for you to become an entrepreneur and to be successful".
To be competitive with the rest of the world we must put some things in place now. I do not think we have time to do so before we recess. We will not block this Bill any more, but we would like to discuss it extensively in committee. We would like to find another solution, because the average citizen, when he reads this Bill and reads his mortgage document, would not understand what the cost is going to be. Give him a fixed sum of money based on certain interest variations. Do not leave it the way it is, because the mortgagee would not know he has a chance of losing his home if the interest rate goes up beyond a certain point.
I appreciate the opportunity to speak on this Bill, Mr. Speaker. I am concerned about Canadian ownership and I would like to see this Bill in committee so that we can review it and come up with a solution.

Mr. Speaker, in speaking briefly to Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Interest Act, I would first of all like to read briefly from the explanatory note to the Bill as it appears in Clause 2 on page la of Bill C-36, and I quote:
Clause 2: These amendments would require certain terms of mortgages on real property to be disclosed if any interest and certain charges are to be payable on or with respect to any money secured thereby. These amendments would also provide a new statutory right to prepay moneys secured by mortgages on real property and further provide that prepayment charges can be recovered only if they are disclosed in the required manner.
That is one of the items in the Bill before us, Mr. Speaker, and of course this Bill is very limited in its impact, but it does
Interest Act
do some things. It can perhaps be said that it is an example of the classic definition of a Liberal, which is that a Liberal is a person who believes in reform as long as it does not cost him or her anything; in other words, the impression and perception of change without any real substance. From now on, thanks to Bill C-36, an Act to amend the Interest Act, when a home owner finds himself or herself, due to a change in rates, faced with the choice of prepaying moneys secured by a mortgage on real property, he or she will have less call to complain legitimately about the cost. He will at least be required to be told in advance what the cost of any penalties will be. In that sense it will be a plus in terms of the fact that it is a public relations job for the banking industry and the trust companies. Home owners may still get shafted, but at least they will have the right to see the shaft coming. It is also, to be fair, a concession to the rights of the public and consumers to know. That is a plus, albeit perhaps a minor plus, to the Bill.
No one can oppose it and no one in the House will be opposing it. There will perhaps be some attempts at change, slight adjustments, but the Bill is of course doing nothing, nor does it pretend to, to solve the interest rate crisis looming once again before Canadians. Interest rates have again been rising in the last few weeks to the same astronomical levels which caused the electoral defeat of the Conservative Government in 1979. They refused to act at that time to protect Canadians, just as the Liberal Government has been refusing to act to protect Canadians in the last few months. They failed even more miserably going back to the period of the absolutely devastating rates of 1981 and 1982.
My colleagues and I in the NDP made a number of proposals over the last few months, and I do not intend to repeat them now. There is no point. We will be raising this subject again, and our proposals to attempt to deal with the interest rate crisis, with the electorate over the next few months. I do not think anything I could say now would convince the Government or the Official Opposition to act in a way other than the way they have acted over the last five years. Their record has been one of failure.
In any case I will not take up any more time of the House at this juncture except to say that here we are getting the appearance, but no real action. It will not stop anyone from being shafted, but at least they may be able to see the shaft coming. I suppose that is a bit of a plus and we ought to be thankful for small mercies.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address a very few remarks to this Bill which will be going from here to committee. I think that is the very least that should happen to it. The Bill is symbolic of what is wrong with this Government. What is the Liberal Government's approach to the question of the right of people to prepay interest on their mortgage loans? It is this abomination, this bureaucratic, mind-boggling, impossibly complicated abomination. We have to say to ourselves that we are simply passing this legislation in the last stages of a dying Parliament because

June 26, 1984
Interest Act
this is the best shot the Liberal Government can give to a very serious problem. When I look at this Bill it is obvious that it will take every Rhodes scholar who ever came from Canada to explain what the Liberal Government had in mind with respect to this legislation.
The Bill removes a very simply concept with respect to existing prepayment provisions. Everyone in this country understands that after five years a mortgagor has the right to prepay the amount of his loan with three month's interest as a bonus. Under this legislation the whole thing is now committed to regulatory law. It makes you wonder what these people are thinking about.
I was interested to hear the NDP point of view again with respect to interest rate policy. I remember when the NDP stood cheek by jowl with the Liberal Party in their traditional role of support. At election time they always try to make sounds as if they were moving separate and apart from the Liberal Party, but they were there to help bring down a government at a time when they said the interest rates were at an unacceptable level. They were there standing by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Gray) when he said that anyone in government who had any principles would resign if interest rates exceeded 14 per cent. That is what he said he would do if he were part of any government which allowed interest rates to escalate to what? I think they were 13 per cent at the time I was part of the Government. There they were, the Liberals and the NDP, conspiring together. This is outrageous, the NDP said, and supported the Liberals in bringing down our Government. Now they are trying to dissociate themselves from the Government. But where were they when interest rates went up to 22 per cent? These people were still supporting the Liberals on every important vote.
I only mention this to put things into perspective, because I think the previous speaker may have left the impression that somehow he was "Simon Pure" with respect to the matter of support of the Liberal Party. I do not want to put too much of a blot on the record of the NDP by bringing these facts out. But we should remember these facts, because the people of Canada remember what that Party did to a sane and reasonable government with a sane approach to the interest problems of this country.
There is apprehension and concern on the part of the average Canadian about the future of interest rates in this country. People across Canada with mortgages on their homes have every right to be concerned. Interest rates in the U.S. will have an impact here. The Minister of State for Finance (Mr. MacLaren) has been very vocal about the suggestion that we are the slave of what happens down in the U.S. and we have absolutely no ability to protect Canadians. If American interest rates go up, we stand ready, aye ready, to follow. Well, we know what is happening in the U.S. and we know what has happened with this Liberal Government. Interest rates went up to 22 per cent, a fantastic level. We know the hardship that caused many people. We know they were put in an impossible situation. Now the Liberal Government has spoken with the approval of its new leader. I am sure Mr. Turner must have been consulted on whether this Bill should go forward in its
present form. If I were Mr. Turner, I would be looking at the legislation package for the end of the session and saying, I will take that one, and kill that. I will take this one, and kill that. I am sure the Government has gone through that consultation process. If they have not, Mr. Turner will still not be able to say that this belongs to another government, another era, and he had no part of this. Ele is leader now, this legislation is his best shot on mortgage interest policy in this country, and I hope that when the election takes place this summer we will not have the unfortunate scene of Mr. Turner trying to say, "well, this is all part of the Trudeau era, I have other ideas." It will not wash. Mr. Turner is in control of the Party and if he said this Bill was not to go through, it would not go through.
We have some very serious concerns about this legislation. It is muddying the waters. The people of Canada should not expect these proposals to be anything more than a panacea for the difficulties they face. In fact, I suggest it is going to complicate their lives. People who have mortgages will not have their expectations met. It was pointed out by a number of my colleagues that this legislation has serious defects. No one has any objection to disclosure; what the people of Canada want is a simple formula which will let them know what their rights are on prepayment. They do not want some cockamamie piece of paper which says that some bureaucrat somewhere in the bowels of Ottawa is going to devise a set of rules to allow them to somehow know what their rights are or what their mortgage interest rates are going to be. We now have smoke and mirrors. This Bill personifies pretty well what is wrong with the Liberal Government. It is beyond belief that the government Members would bring this Bill forward at this point in time in the session. We will let them have their best shot. We will put it through to committee. We will be asking some hard questions in committee. We will expect the Minister to be there with his officials to explain what this means and how this is going to be of any assistance at all to the mortgage holders of Canada. There is concern.
One way that the people of Canada will be able to get good legislation through with respect to various problems is to have a real change. They do not want a cosmetic change or a Liberal Party with a new leader. They want a new administration that is going to deal in a responsible manner with respect to two elements. A Progressive Conservative Government will let people know what their rights are, in very simple legislative terms, in terms of prepayment of their mortgages. Not only will the people know, the people involved in the mortgage business will have a very clear legislative direction.
All the people sitting on the Liberal benches will be able to watch Parliament after the next election from their living rooms in their own home constituencies. I want them to understand that we tried to tell them that this legislation is not adequate to meet the problems faced by people with escalating interest rates on the mortgages on their homes. We tried to be constructive. We tried to tell them to come to their senses before it was too late. We will pass this legislation if the
June 26, 1984

Government wants to ram it through with its majority. We will deal with the matter. We are not going to be obstructive. It seems to me that this is an indication that the Government has run out of ideas and perspective. It is out of touch with the Canadian people. If the Government had consulted with the Canadian people and found out what they were saying, this abomination would never have been presented to Parliament for swift consideration. We tried to tell them what to do and we tried to be helpful. Regrettably, Mr. Speaker, this is their best effort. We will have the matter go to committee, at which time we will have some questions to ask and some positions to put forward. If this is the best they can offer, it is a sad commentary on the kind of Government they are presenting to the Canadian people.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Are there questions or comments? For debate, the Hon. Member for Kootenay East-Revelstoke.

Mr. Speaker, I too wish to participate in debate on Bill C-36, and Act to amend the Interest Act. Clause 2 of the explanatory notes reads:
These amendments would require certain terms of mortgages on real property to be disclosed if any interest and certain charges are to be payable on or with respect to any money secured thereby.
I listened with interest to the Member for Saskatoon West (Mr. Hnatyshyn). It was interesting to note that he tied the New Democratic Party with the Liberals. In fact the newly elected Leader of the Conservative Party was a director of the Bank of Commerce. The newly elected Leader of the Liberal Party also served as a director of the Bank of Commerce.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: You are wrong.
Well, one of the major banks. There are very close ties in industry as well as in banking.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Get your facts straight and come back later.

There are ties with one of the major banks. We see some very close ties there. Until we start to address the problems with regard to mortgages and interest rates, those are the kinds of ties that will have to be addressed. We see political Parties tied with major banks and major industries through directorships. How is the ordinary individual going to get anyone to stand up in the House and really address the question of interest rates?
The Conservative Party and the Liberal Party are the same. They are the same as they are in British Columbia where the Liberals and the Conservatives sit together and call themselves Social Credit. This afternoon we are debating interest rates. It is a token program introduced by a dying Government in the last stages of our session. It is a token program to address this very urgent and pressing requirement of the Canadian people. Mortgage interest rates must be addressed in a positive way. There is only one way it can be done, that is, through the Bank of Canada. Mr. Bouey of the Bank of Canada and the Canadian Government must come up with a policy setting out
Interest Act
mortgage rates as they were after the war when the Veterans Act was passed and special consideration was given to mortgage rates. If it could be done then, it can be done now.
As elected people we can sit down and develop a program through the Bank of Canada. Our problems lie in the fact that the Leader of the Official Opposition and the newly elected Leader of the Liberal Party have histories of sitting on the boards of directors of major industries and major banks in Canada. We must recognize that Canadian people need affordable housing. Interest rates must be such that when mortgages are taken out the people will have confidence that they will be able to carry them through.
We talk about interest rates. We talk about the various governments and their policies and we talk about equality. Where is the equality in people not being able to live in affordable housing in Canada with proper interest rates? Where is the equality in someone being forced out of his home because of a Government that does not recognize that a person's home is his sanctuary? There must be a program put in place to meet those financial needs. Mortgage interest rates must be kept at affordable levels. There is virtually no protection of any long-standing nature in this Bill. When are we going to present something concrete which will allow people to enter a long-term mortgage with the confidence that they will be able to fulfil that agreement?
Until we address that problem and separate the Leader of the Official Opposition and the newly elected Leader of the Government from their ties with the corporate structure and the banking industry, we are going to be faced with this kind of problem. This Bill will not address that. We strongly oppose this kind of measure which really has no significance to any of our people.
Questions or comments? Debate? Is the House ready for the question?
Yes.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want the House or anyone to be under any misapprehension. The Government House Leader (Mr. Pinard) clearly stated the order of business today. I responded by saying that it was satisfactory.
There has been no consultation or discussion about dealing with any other items of legislation. Of course, we are prepared to proceed on the basis of having some advance knowledge about government Bills that are supposedly coming up. There was no back-up Bill with respect to the Bank Act.
The Government House Leader was quite clear and unequivocal. He has not consulted with me about any other legislation. To be quite frank, I asked him what would happen if we finished before nine o'clock and he said that will be the end of the day.
1 do not want it to be laid at my Party's doorstep that we are not prepared to work. We are prepared to work in the interest of Canadians morning, noon and night. We will consent to it, but it is not because we are not prepared to sit here.
